subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL

speechtext:
Hon. G. D. HOWE (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 21, to amend the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in bringing down
this measure I feel I am sponsoring a most important and necessary piece of legislation. It is common knowledge that the three directors to whom the direction of the railways was entrusted as a result of the 1933 act have made no real progress toward the improvement of our railway situation. To date they have failed to achieve any substantial cooperative economies, to secure which was the principal object of their appointment and the outstanding feature of the 1933 legislation. Not only have they failed to secure any substantial results to date, but on their own published statements, the prospect of future results from cooperative measures, plans and arrangements is not bright. Nor have they been able to reduce to any great extent Canadian National operating costs, due to the fact that that avenue had been so thoroughly explored by the previous boards of directors. I shall in a few moments support these statements by citations from the reports of the trustees themselves. That is the external situation.
Internally, as most hon. members are probably aware, there is much unrest among Canadian National employees who everywhere appear to regard the trustee method of direction and control with distrust and suspicion. This is primarily due to the fact that in matters of actual management the chief operating officer with the titular rank of president is subordinated to a trustee

C.N.R.-Board o/ Directors
board of three laymen, inexperienced in railway problems and who know nothing of actual railway practice, and, as a result, have shown a complete lack of understanding of the human element which, under prevailing conditions, enters so largely into successful railway operation. In talking over the situation with the trustees themselves I cannot find that any one of them believes that the present system of management is a good one. As things stand the trustee board is responsible to no one, is apparently without a policy, and. so far as public relations are concerned, is without even a voice. In addition, there is, to put it mildly, serious lack of agreement among the trustees themselves, and the fate of any measure with which they must deal depends upon whether one of the other trustees can be brought to agree with the views of the chairman, who is vested with overriding authority in that a majority vote of the trustees is ineffective unless the chairman be included in that majority.
That the trustee arrangement would not work was clearly recognized by the Liberal opposition when the 1933 bill was under debate in this chamber. At that time the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) took the ground that a ministry could not divest itself of responsibility for the direction and control of the Canadian National Railways, as was contemplated by the act, nor could parliament abrogate its duty. However, the 1933 bill became law and the government of the day set up the trustee form of management and direction largely on the basis of the existence of what was described as a "receivership situation" with respect to the national lines, the object of which was to bring about "an equilibrium between income and expenditure" and restore the railway to a position where it could earn its way.
Two years have passed since the trustees were given complete authority to accomplish this most desirable aim, and I doubt whether anyone in this house will assert that what has been accomplished by the trustee form of direction and control could not have been accomplished equally well if not better by the board of directors who were displaced by the trustees.
In 1933 Canadian National revenues touched an all time low. Such increase in operating surplus as has resulted since 1933 has been due to increase in traffic or to economies introduced by the displaced board of directors rather than to improvements in administrative policy or practice inaugurated by the trustees. As a matter of fact, the former boards of directors had done very good work in the curtailment of expenditures and the
adoption of measures of economy before the board of trustees appeared on the scene. That they had been efficient in that respect is shown by the following extract from the annual report issued by the board of trustees for the year 1934 at the end of their first year in office:
During the year studies have been made in numerous directions in the effort to secure the maximum economy in the operation of all departments. The severe decline in gross revenue had made it imperative that all opportunities for economy be closely examined and re-examined, and the drastic curtailment of all expenditures effected prior to 1934 testifies to the vigorous steps taken. Further economies necessarily became difficult to secure if the efficiency of the service was to be maintained.
As to "cooperative measures, plans and arrangements," the board of trustees require 2,000 words to explain why more had not been accomplished. The Canadian Pacific covered the same ground in 250 words of the directors' report, which concluded as follows:
The total annual joint economy secured by the two companies from the measures put into effect up to the end of 1934 is estimated to be $1,220,510.
That estimate has by the 1935 report of the Canadian Pacific Railway been placed at §1,600,000, one half of which will accrue to each company. That sum includes the economies secured by the former board of directors, as the two railways did not wait for the 1933 bill to become law before taking action in the matter of joint economies. As to this I will quote the following brief extracts from the annual report of the Canadian National Railways for that year, 1933, addressed to the board of trustees by Mr. Hungerford, as acting president, and forwarded by the trustees to the Minister of Railways for presentation to parliament:
In accordance with the expressed desire of parliament, the managements of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways took action in November 1932 toward effecting cooperative economies before the enactment of the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act of 1933. Results so far accomplished are evidenced in the partial pooling of passenger train services between Montreal and Toronto and Ottawa and Toronto. Other economies have resulted from arrangements for joint operations, such as switching, car cleaning and freight shed operation at a number of points where duplication existed, as well as the hauling of traffic by one railway for the other. Many similar projects are under study.
In view of the meagre results it is not surprising that the trustees thought it necessary to include in their 1934 report the following explanation as to why greater results had not been secured:	. [DOT]
Joint examination of many projects which superficially appeared capable of yielding CO-
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

operative economies showed that the economies to be derived are not commensurate with the capital expenditures necessary to bring them about, or that under present conditions no economy would result, a condition fundamentally due to the fact that measures already taken individually by each railroad to meet the conditions imposed by the depression had curtailed services to an irreducible minimum.
Since the present -bill was drafted the annual report of Canadian National Railways for the year 1935 has been brought down. This report deals at great length with cooperative measures, plans and arrangements by the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways, and once more the trustees are unable to report any substantial progress. They refer to the large amount of "investigational work" by joint committees of the two companies, but "the amount of preliminary detail has proved to be so great that no additional cooperative measures have been made effective." The report states however that the research work "has indicated possibilities of further economies, more particularly in the matter of functionally duplicate line abandonments and joint facility arrangements, and efforts are now being concentrated along these lines." To quote from the 1935 report:
The question of further extending the area of passenger train pooling has been under study during the past year by the joint technical committee and conclusion has been reached that the economy possible of attainment at this time is not sufficient to warrant the expenditure of capital required to make the principal passenger train terminals suitable for joint use and to offset disruption in traffic which would necessarily be involved.
Similarly the trustees report inability, for reasons which they cite, to reduce the number of city ticket offices maintained by the two companies, and then go on to state that the United States legislation of 1933, the general purpose of which was similar to the Canadian act of that year, had failed to produce any definite coordination measures to date:
This further evidences the difficulties inherent in bringing such measures into effect. The British railways met with similar difficulties.
The trustees return to the subject towards the conclusion of their report, when they state:
Some further economy from cooperative measures may be expected but cooperative economy is a most difficult process when maintenance expenditures and train and car mileage have been so drastically reduced. It is becoming increasingly certain that any substantial improvement in net earnings can be secured in no other way than by increased volume of traffic and, in the opinion of the trustees, it is in the public interest that the way out of the present difficulties be found in 
an expansion of earnings rather than by way of a further curtailment of railway expenditures.
Two annual reports from the Canadian National trustees, but one continuous recitation of apologies for lack of success in applying the cooperative provisions of the 1933 act under which they were appointed. The results have been disappointing, and I venture to say they have been disappointing to the hon. gentlemen opposite who were responsible for the appointment of the trustees whose regime was intended to bring about an equilibrium between income and expenditure. The right hon. leader of the opposition himself evidently was not hopeful of the success of trustee direction and control, because toward the end of the late campaign he announced that it was proposed to undertake still another inquiry into transportation in Canada, including railways-the third in comparatively recent years. That proposal could scarcely be regarded as a vote of confidence in the ability of the trustees to do what was expected of them.
I think it can be shown also that the right hon. leader of the opposition himself had some reason to question the degree of authority which the 1933 act placed in the hands of the trustees, and there is evidence also that his Minister of Railways had reason to feel that his position had been rendered very unsatisfactory by the 1933 measure. I am brought to that conclusion by a perusal of statements made by the chairman of the board of trustees before the standing committee of this house which deals with Canadian National accounts and estimates, the recorded proceedings of which show that in the discussion of the recommendations of Touche and Company concerning the capital structure of the railway, no action had been taken by the trustees because of a certain letter received from the then Prime Minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: That was all put on record later in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Quite. I do not want to dwell on that.
The Liberal opposition was not alone in expressing doubts as to the success of the 1933 legislation. The railwaymen of Canada, as represented by eighteen railway organizations, and the trades and labour congress, prepared an extensive memorandum of comments and recommendations which were placed before the senate committee which dealt with the 1933 legislation before it was brought into this chamber. These representations were to the effect that a board of trustees consisting of three persons would not be sufficient

CNJt.-Board oj Directors
properly to look after the affairs of so vast a property as the Canadian National system, and they recommended a board of at least five trustees. They were particularly concerned about the problems involving the human element, and considered that at least one member of the new board of trustees, regardless of its size, should be specially qualified to counsel in respect to these problems by reason of his experience and the confidence imposed in him by the railway employees. They pointed out that the policy had been recognized in the appointment of the previous directors by both Liberal and Conservative governments, and to that arrangement was attributed much of the loyalty and enthusiasm as well as the good relations between the management and the men on the Canadian National railways, which had been specially referred to in the Duff report. In the setting up of the board of trustees these views of railway labour were not considered.
Railway labour also objected to the veto power proposed to be vested in the chairman, which, it was felt, would in practice subject him to the temptation of dictatorship. It was regarded as too great a concentration of responsibility and authority in one man.
The difficulties foreseen by these railway representatives have been verified by actual experience. The board of trustees clearly is not representative enough, and the powers granted the chairman have endowed him practically with autocratic authority, the result of which is that, while you have a board of three trustees, it is really a one-man affair. In the circumstances the wonder is that others should be willing to accept appointment to the trustee board with their views and opinions discounted and even nullified in advance.
The reading of the recommendation of the Duff commission, with respect to the board of trustees, admits of no doubt as to the calibre of the men the royal commission had in mind for trusteeship:
All should be persons of proved business skill and capacity;
The chairman in particular should have financial, administrative and executive ability of a high order.
Those were the specifications laid down by the Duff commission. Possibly the recommendation was a counsel of perfection which the then government could not realize. Admittedly it is not easy to enlist the services of executives of that type, and although the 1933 legislation came into force on the first day of July of that year, the appointment of the trustee board was not made until the end of the year, when an order in council was passed appointing Honourable C. P.
Fullerton, K.C., to be chairman, and Frederick K. Morrow, of Toronto, and J. Edouard La-belle, K.C., of Montreal, to be trustees-twyo lawyers, and the third a company director. Both the latter had had a couple of years' experience on the board of directors of Canadian National Railways, but the chairman had had no previous experience in railway management, and while he had no doubt very useful qualifications for the bench or for the board of railway commissioners, his training and experience did not suggest that he possessed the "financial, administrative and executive ability " specified by the royal commission as a prime requisite for chairmanship of the board of trustees. Into the hands of such a board of trustees the act of 1933 delivered the fortunes of the Canadian National Railways- a body of three laymen, only one of whom was permitted an effective voice; not one of the three having any knowledge of actual railway practice, or experience in the handling of the human element, which enters so largely into railway operation.
One of the first acts of this board of trustees was to carry out that provision of the 1933 bill which requires the appointment of a chief operating officer "with titular rank of president," responsible to, and reporting to, the board of trustees and to that board alone, and to pass a by-law setting out his duties. My reading of the legislation, and particularly of the Duff report on which it is based, leads me to believe that the legislation intended that the president should be the operating head of the railway, in fact as well as in name, but this, it seems, was not the view of the trustees. After I assumed office, the chairman himself gave me his interpretation of the legislation, which was that it was intended that the operating head should be president in name only and that his real position was intended to be that of vice-president of the operating department.
The "powers, authorities and duties" of the chief operating officer, with titular rank of president, were defined by by-law of the board of trustees of January 31, 1934, and practical railwaymen will appreciate the fact that in enumerating the duties of the president in the management of the railway's transportation and communication services, the by-law states-"including, for example, the fixing of time schedules and conditions in connection therewith."
Having assigned the fixing of time schedules to the chief operating officer, with the titular rank of president, the by-law further provided that his duties should include:
The engaging and continuing in and discharging from employment, the personnel
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

required for such purposes, or any of them, and the fixing of the terms and conditions of such employment, all salaries to be approved by the chairman of the trustees. This authority, however, is not to cover the appointment of vice-presidents, general managers, secretary, treasurer, European agent, European secretary treasurer, or heads of departments.
Such a state of affairs as reserving to the board of trustees or the chairman of it the authority to reward by way of salary and promotion could have no other effect than to weaken the position of the president as chief operating officer. In general, the man holding the title of president-admittedly one of the ablest railway executives in North America, who, in his forty-five years of service with Canadian railways, has risen from the lowest to the highest rung in the railway ladder- has had his position reduced to that of adviser to the chairman, who has made himself the real operating head of the railway property.
The Duff report, paragraph 209, definitely recommended that "the responsibility for the direction and control of the system should be laid upon the chairman and his associate trustees," but it was also explicitly stated that under the chief operating officer with the titular rank of president "should be placed the entire working of the railway in detail." In conformity with this recommendation, section 10 of the 1933 act provided that the trustees should appoint:
. . . on terms to be fixed by them and with the titular rank of president, a person other than one of themselves to execute and perform, under and in consultation with them, the powers, authorities and duties of chief operating officer of national railways, as such powers, authorities and duties shall be from time to time defined by by-law and resolution of the trustees and committed for execution and performance.
It seems to me that any reasonable man would assume from this that it was the intention that the trustees should confine themselves to matters of policy, particularly in the direction of economies, with respect to which they were specifically enjoined by parts II and III of the Trustee Act, and that the "financial, administrative and executive ability" required of the chairman should be devoted to matters of broad policy. On the other hand it seems obvious that the operation of the railway in all its details was intended to be placed in the hands of an experienced railroad executive.
This intention was obviously not apparent to the chairman of the trustees, who proceeded to divide the offices of the railway into two camps, one responsible to the chairman and the other to the president. In that division of offices the chairman took over for operation by himself the following departments: legal,

finance and accounting, publicity, medical, colonization, land and property, secretary's branch, hotels and1 steamships, and assumed joint direction with the president over the purchasing and stores departments. The fact that the chairman was totally inexperienced in matters affecting any of these departments, except possibly the legal department, did not deter him in the least.
Under the president were placed the departments of traffic, operation and construction economic, personnel, investigation, industrial, express, telegraphs, office services, statistics and pass bureau.
Under this arrangement the chief operating officer of the railway has been deprived of contact with and authority over departments which are an important and essential part of railway operation, such as the law offices and the financial and accounting departments. The fact that he has no control of the publicity department may explain why in recent years Canadian National publicity has failed to place before the people of Canada many of the things that should have been made known with respect to Canadian National Railways.
Having indicated the directions in which the appointment of trustees has failed to realize the expectations associated with the 1933 bill, I will deal briefly with the general provisions of the amendments to the act as contained in the bill now under consideration. I appreciate that consideration of the details of the bill will come in committee of the whole on the bill. However, it is sufficient, perhaps, to say that the present bill does not change the intent and purpose of the 1933 measure other than to the extent necessary to provide for the substitution of a board of seven directors for the present board of three trustees. Some explanation is in order as to why the number is fixed at seven. To limit the directors to three, as in the case of the trustees, would be to invite a repetition of some of the present difficulties, as even were each of the three to be accorded equal voice and vote there would be too great a centralization of authority in the direction of so vast an organization. The Drayton-Acworth recommendation of 1917 was for five trustees, including three railway members, one member to be selected on the ground of business and financial experience, and one as specially possessing the confidence of railway employees.
The Canadian National Railway Act of 1919 provided for a board of not less than five and not more than fifteen directors. That act was amended in 1931 to provide for two additional directors, making seventeen in all. The contact of such a widely scattered directorate, meeting monthly, was found to

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
be not sufficiently direct and continuous. To improve matters, an executive committee of six directors within easy reach of Montreal was set up in 1927; increased to seven in 1930, and to eight in 1931, when a finance committee of three directors (members of the executive committee) was also established. I mention these matters to show that the former directorate was found in practice to be unwieldy and cumbersome, and that an effort had been made to improve matters by centralizing the executive direction and control in the hands of a committee approximating in numbers those provided for by the present bill. The number is small enough to permit selection of men of proven worth and outstanding ability, and large enough to bring a variety of experience to bear upon important railway problems.
The present bill provides that the governor in council shall appoint the directors and also appoint one of their number to be chairman. A majority of the directors will govern, instead of the present trustee provision that the vote of the chairman is required before a decision can pass. This government will make a strong effort to secure men of "proven business skill and capacity," and it is intended to return to the practice, departed from in the case of the trustees, of placing on the board an outstanding representative of organized labour. It is the intention of the government to appoint as chairman a trained and experienced railway man, one not only thoroughly conversant with the Canadian National railway system and its problems but one who understands the human element, which enters so largely into successful railway operation.
It is not the intention to reappoint the deputy minister of railways to the board of directors. If it were considered desirable to do so, the present deputy minister of railways has very excellent qualifications for the post, by training and experience not only with the Canadian National, but with other railways, and as a professor of transportation at McGill for some years. The decision of the government, therefore, involves no reflection upon the present deputy minister of railways, but merely indicates that the government intends to appoint a board of directors and then permit it to function without necessity to have regard to the presence at the directors' table of one who may be assumed to represent the view of the government upon such matters as may be under discussion, as to which the government is properly concerned with policy only. The government intends to see to it that the 12739-140
directors are in a position to discuss freely and among themselves any and all matters coming before them.
The government believe, however, that it is very necessary for the Minister of Railways to work in harmony and in close contact with the chairman of the board of directors because of the problems that constantly arise as affecting government and railway policy, which matters cannot be dealt with adequately by the directors unless they know authoritatively the policy and intention of the government with respect to the matter at issue. The government will not again be satisfied to be wise after the event. If it is obliged to carry responsibility for the national railways, as it must, it is necessary that it should be in close touch with railway policy and have a voice in the shaping of that policy, as it is the government which must find the money for railway purposes. Whatever contact with the board may be necessary to keep the government in touch with railway policy and the railway property will, therefore, be as between the chairman of the board of directors and the Minister of Railways direct.
The government have given careful thought to the question of tenure of the board of directors. As to that there are a number of considerations involved. For the board of trustees the Duff commission recommended a tenure of seven years, with provision for a measure of continuity by staggering the terms of the initial appointees. The 1933 act restricted the tenure to five years, and for purposes of continuity the chairman was appointed for five, Mr. Morrow for four, and Mr. Labelle for three years. It is the intention of the present bill to establish a tenure of three years, and three of the original directors will be appointed for that term, two for two years, and two for one year terms; subsequent appointments of all to be for three year periods. In this way provision is made for necessary continuity by annual rotation of a portion of the board, which is the practice followed by many large corporations, notably the Canadian Pacific Railway. All appointments to the board will of course be by the governor in council, but it is hoped that reasonable permanency will be assured by the modified tenure proposed, and by the process of rotation, but most of all through the outstanding merit of the appointments to be made.
As to executive direction, I may say quite frankly that the government can see a certain merit in having the office of chairman held by one man and the office of president held by another, provided the president is made



Board oj Directors

the real operating head of the railway, and provided the president and chairman can work in complete harmony, with the president attending to all matters of operation and the chairman confining himself to matters of policy and public relations. Therefore provision is being made in this legislation for combining the offices of chairman and president, and for the separating of the two offices as the directors may decide and as personnel available for these two important offices will permit. It is felt that best results can be obtained if the chairman himself could be allowed to train and develop the man who will occupy the office of president, and it is therefore intended that the two offices shall be combined until such time as it is reasonably certain that they can be divided without endangering the operating efficiency of the railway.
I am aware that the Duff commission did not recommend the appointment of a present officer of the Canadian National Railways to the post of chairman, or as trustee; also that the commission recommended that any senator, member of parliament or former office holder be disqualified for appointment as trustee. Appointment of senators or members would scarcely be urged, but in other respects it seems to me that the action of the royal commission was contrary to well established precedent and the rules of common sense. Most of the successful industries in Canada or elsewhere are headed by a chief executive who grew up with the business. It sometimes happens that a business does not produce an executive who is competent to direct its policies, and that an outsider has to be brought in, but almost invariably this outsider is one trained in the same line of business. Fortunately Canadian National Railways have a man who is not only outstanding as a railway executive but has the respect of the Canadian people and of railway labour, and the confidence of this government. The 1933 legislation eliminated that part of the Duff report which specifically debarred holders or former holders of public office; the present bill removes the disability which would operate against employees of Canadian National Railways in the selection of chief executive.
The present bill provides for the approval of the governor in council, when by law approval of the shareholders of a company is required, instead of dispensing with any such approval by either the governor in council or shareholders, as was done in the 1933 bill. This is but right and proper, as the government are the elected representatives of the owners of the national railways, and there can be no question as to the mandate.

The act of 1933 was in four parts. Part I dealt with the trustees, and hon. gentlemen will note that the amendments contained in the proposed bill have to do almost entirely with this part of the 1933 measure, and are intended to effect a substitution of a board of seven directors for the board of three trustees.
Part II of the 1933 act enjoins upon -the two railways the duty of attempting "forthwith to agree and continuously to endeavour to agree" upon "cooperative measures, plans and arrangements." I have already dealt at length with the failure of the trustees, on their own admission, to achieve any great-result under this section. They are not very hopeful of further economies, but tell us that the field of cooperative effort is still being explored, and if there still remain possibilities of worth while savings through cooperative efforts it is the desire of the government that they be secured. Before passing judgment on the practicability of Part II, it would, I think, be well to have the situation reviewed by the board of directors which will succeed the trustees. The substitution of the word "directors" for the word "trustees" is therefore the only change made in Part II of the 1933 act.
Part III of the act provides for compulsory arbitration by the chief commissioner of the board of railway commissioners. While Part III has never been invoked, and it is rather unlikely that it will be, we are leaving that in the aot.
Part IV of the 1933 act definitely provides against amalgamation of the two railways, or unified management and control, and that feature is also being reenacted without change.
I have dealt somewhat fully with the difference betwreen the board of directors as now proposed and the board of trustees. In case it may be suggested that the present bill returns the Canadian National Railways to the same form of direction that obtained under the late Sir Henry Thornton, I would point out that the situation is materially different. Sir Henry Thornton as managing head had a direct contract with the government, the last one covering a five year period. He therefore spoke with the voice of the government. The Department of Railways maintained a connection with the Thornton board in the person of the deputy minister, and was thus in a position to influence the board and the managing head-who was also chairman and president, by election-whether on matters of high government policy, or on matters of operation, with which the government properly was not concerned.

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
The present bill is intended to afford a much greater measure of autonomy to the chairman and board of directors. There will be no one at the directors' table other than the seven directors themselves. Such contact between the government and the board as may be necessary in the public interest will be provided by conference between the chairman and the Minister of Railways as and when questions arise where the intentions of the railway should be made known to the government and the views of the government should be declared to the directors. There will be no question about that contact or the medium of it. It is in effect the essence of the present legislation, for reasons already adduced, which it is not necessary to repeat.
The new board will differ from previous boards also in other important respects. The contact of the former boards of directors was casual rather than continuous, and it is proposed that the coming board shall take a much more active and effective part in the administration of the affairs of the railway.
Benefiting from past experience, the government will avoid the mistake of appointing too elaborate a board, with its invitation to political and public pressure, which the Duff commission reprehended. It will in the first instance appoint the chairman and president in one person. As and when a president, other than one of the directors, is chosen chief executive officer, he will be appointed by the board, subject to the approval of the governor in council. The directors and salaried officers will be each paid but a single remuneration, no matter how many subsidiary boards of the Canadian National system they may find themselves on. The present bill is thus not intended to reestablish the old order.
May I add that in my opinion the provisions of this proposed bill are of great importance. There can be no doubt that this government has a mandate to do its utmost to improve the operating position of Canadian National Railways so that there may be an end to the deficits that are so harmful to the credit of Canada. In this it must have the assistance and cooperation of an executive possessed of all the ability and experience that can be brought to bear upon the problem. Unfortunately the trustees have not been able to bring to bear either the ability or the experience contemplated by the Duff commission. No doubt they have done their best, but that best falls far short of the Duff commission concept of the administrative requirements of the national lines, and in the making of the appointments the late government either lost sight of the commission's
recommendations or were unable to secure men of the calibre the Duff commission had in mind when it advised that all three trustees should be persons of proved business skill and capacity, and that the chairman in particular should have financial, administrative and executive ability of a high order. The chairmanship was the key post, and failure at that point has been fatal to the success of the trustee plan as a whole. That failure has been aggravated by the inability of the chairman properly to interpret his own duties and responsibilities in the light of either the 193f act or the Duff report. The act called for the appointment of a chief operating officer other than one of the trustees, but in practice we find the chairman of the board of trustees usurping powers appertaining to the chief operating officer, in whose hands the Duff report recommended should be placed the entire working of the railway. There has thus been a progressive departure all down the line from the high ideals of direction and management contemplated by the Duff commission, and it has been amply demonstrated that the board of trustees, regardless of intentions, is incapable of meeting the situation, and that their lack of knowledge of railway administration acts as a wet blanket and dampens the ardour and enthusiasm of a railway staff which in former days distinguished itself, and which, properly led, will be able to go on to still greater achievements. To be effective, reorganization of the railway management must start from the top, but without the legislation now proposed this government will be helpless to effect the reforms so obviously needed I have attempted to deal with the situatior fairly and to present this measure in such a manner as to command consideration on its merits, divorced from any considerations of party advantage. Such criticism as I have directed to the working out of the 1933 measure has, I hope, been reasonably void of offence to hon. gentlemen who, three years ago, attempted in good faith to give effect to the recommendations of the royal commission. That those plans and arrangements have failed to effect the purpose intended is not a matter of gratification on the part of anybody. As already expressed, it is my personal belief, after close study and investigation, that the trustee plan is unworkable, and that it has shown itself to be so. I believe that the proposals contained in the present bill, in which, as it should be, account is taken of past mistakes, we have a much better plan, one much more in keeping with the principles of responsible government, and for which, in conclusion, I would request the careful consideration of hon. members on both sides of the house, having

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
regard to the fact that the railway problem is not a party question, nor ought it to be, but a matter of business of vital concern to every Canadian citizen.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the temptation to follow the political address of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Howe) is very great. The first few minutes of his speech was of such an acrimonious and political character that I find it difficult to recall myself to the duty which I owe to myself and the country, which far transcends in importance the answering of the speech to which we have just listened. To indict a man upon his removal from office in his absence and without opportunity to be heard, has not been the usual practice in parliament. The statute that placed the chairman in office provides for his removal. It provides that he can be removed only by joint address of both houses of parliament, which, of course, involves an opportunity for him to give his defence against any charges which might be preferred against him.
The minister has seen fit this afternoon to make a series of charges against the chairman, some of which, if warranted by facts, would entirely support a charge being laid against the chairman under the provisions of the section providing for his removal. There is, however, a committee appointed by this house which will have to consider the Canadian National Railway accounts for the past year, and I suggest to the minister that if he expects to get far with this bill the first thing he must do is to call that committee together at the earliest possible moment to afford the chairman an opportunity of presenting his defence in respect of the charges that have been made against him.
So far as the other phase of this matter is concerned, ample reasons were given why, if I were so minded, I should bring to the attention of this house and the country conditions that I think would place the responsibility for the operating situation and the financial position to which the hon. gentleman referred, upon those who were responsible for the creation of the systems of railways in addition to the Canadian Pacific Railway which have brought ruin to this country at the moment. But I content myself with the realization that at the moment I have a responsibility far greater than that. I shall endeavour to discuss this matter as best I can without suggesting responsibility on the part of those now in office or dealing at all with the question of responsibility. I shall endeavour to discuss this terrible situation so far as the railways are concerned as a con-

dition and not a theory, a condition that must be grappled with and must be met if the solvency of this country is to be maintained.
During the five long and weary years of world depression, when the trade of the world had fallen to only thirty per cent of what it was before the depression began-not simply a thirty per cent diminution in trade but a drop in world trade to only thirty per cent of what it was before the depression, and at the darkest moment the figure was 33i per cent-the one great problem that the government of this country had to consider, in addition to the general financial situation and the internal situation of its people, had to do with railway conditions.
I am going to do what is perhaps an unusual thing. In view of the correspondence and the articles that are appearing in the newspapers it is quite clear to me that the people have not had an opportunity to read the report of the so-called Duff commission or to appreciate the facts to which it directs attention. I shall therefore place upon Hansard extracts from that report in order that those who now read at least short resumes of what takes place in parliament will have a clear appreciation and understanding of the facts as found by that commission. But before doing so, instead of reviewing the circumstances that brought about the three transcontinental railway systems, now merged into two, I point out that a commission was appointed, the Dray-ton-Acworth commission, to consider the railway situation and to make a report to the minister. But in 1931 it became apparent that the railway situation was one of extreme gravity. It became more apparent, shall I say, than ever before because of the reports made by the then, chairman, Sir Henry Thornton, to which I shall direct attention presently, as his remarks were recorded and made part of the report, and because of the observations made by the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Both were of the opinion that the government should set up a commission to investigate and study the situation. The reasons they gave were not identical, but they at least reached the same conclusion, namely, that a commission should be appointed to investigate the whole situation for the purpose of seeing what might be done, but not for the purpose of bringing about an equilibrium between income and expenditure within a few months; because no one in those days, any more than does the government of to-day, contemplated the possibility of bringing about that desired end. The very fact that the government the other day desired

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
to make provision for deficits on the Canadian National Railways for the year 1936 indicates that in accordance with the opinion of those responsible for administration the Minister of Finance anticipates there will be a deficit in the Canadian National railway undertaking during the current year. No one in 1931 had any opinion other than that. I concluded, after discusisng the matter with my colleagues at some length on many occasions that it would be desirable to appoint a commission.
The personnel of the commission gave us much difficulty. It is not an easy thing to secure a commission of men who have a clear insight into and understanding of the problems to be dealt with by any commission studying the transportation problem in Canada. We realized that practically the whole of the Canadian Pacific four per cent perpetual debenture stock, and its preference stock, as well as a large share of its common stock, was held in Great Britain. We realized that a very large volume of the securities issued by the Canadian National system when it consisted of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk were held in Great Britain and that there should be on that commission some person whose domicile or home was in Great Britain and who had a clear and, shall I say, comprehensive understanding of the problems connected with transportation and with finance as related to transportation. We were fortunate in securing the services of Lord Ash-field, who was born in the United States and trained in transportation at Detroit, Michigan, and elsewhere in the United States. Finally he had been entrusted with the enormous responsibility of consolidating the transportation services of the city of London and district, comprising the underground, the above ground and the on-the-ground lines, the street railway, the tube, and the bus. About that time he was concluding his efforts, as was indicated by a measure passed by the parliament of the united kingdom a short time afterwards. He decided to come, not because he desired to come but because he believed it was a public duty, having regard to the conditions that existed in this country and which were apparently fairly well known to everybody.
The chairmanship of the commission was very important, and we were fortunate in securing the services of the Chief Justice of Canada. The chief justice has been on the bench for many years, and so far as I know he has no political views, although at one time he was actively associated with the fortunes of the Liberal party in British Columbia. He has held high judicial office
in that province and has made for himself an outstanding name among the great jurists of the world, of which I believe every Canadian is truly proud. Because of the lifelong experience he has had in sifting facts and applying legal principles, he has attained for himself a position equal to but not excelled by the great jurists of the British empire. I have heard this statement made by two gentlemen who were lord chancellors and by others who occupied positions of great responsibility as jurists in the United Kingdom. He undertook the chairmanship of this commission, thereby ensuring, I think, such complete impartiality of inquiry as can come only from one who understands the relationship of testimony and evidence and who is able to sift it and consider it in relation to the facts with which he has to deal.
It was important also that there should be upon the commission a representative of business in the large sense to which the minister has referred. We secured for that purpose the services of Sir Joseph Flavelle and Mr. Beaudry Leman, the latter general manager of the Banque Canadienne Nationale. In their realms of business activities both these gentlemen are held in the highest regard and esteem. Mr. Leman, who had the advantage of training as an engineer, brought to bear upon the problems presented to him the mind and skill not only of a trained engineer but of one who had had much experience in business and was able to appreciate the relation of the solution of the problem to the whole financial structure. Sir Joseph Flavelle has many enemies and many friends, but whatever may be the views of those who oppose or support him, I have never yet met a person who was not prepared to admit the power of his intellect and the strength of his mental equipment in dealing with problems and matters of business. He had had some experience, for he had been chairman of the Grand Trunk Canadian board.
It was felt that we should have a railway man not a Canadian and it was a difficult problem to secure the services of a railway man on the American continent. It is well known that an effort was made to secure the services of the presidents of two of the largest transcontinental systems. They were not available, and we were recommended to apply to the president of the Delaware and Hudson railway. This is not a large railway system, but it is one which has been successful during these dark days. Mr. Loree had made for himself amongst the captains of industry in the neighbouring republic and the great railway executives of the transcontinental systems a reputation that warranted our relying
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

upon him in dealing with problems of this kind. He was good enough to undertake that responsibility.
We felt that it was desirable to have on the commission someone from the maritime provinces who was not actively engaged in political warfare but who knew something of the history and development- of the mari-times and their relation to the general picture so far as railways were concerned. We asked Doctor Webster to accept, and he expressed a willingness to do so. In his youth he was a distinguished student, a graduate of one of the smaller universities in the maritimes. In his work in the medical department of the great university of Edinburgh he attained a position of prominence which enabled him a little later to become one of the foremost in his 'branch of medical science in the city of Chicago. When fortune had smiled upon him and he had reached the age at which it is said a great physician intimated a man should retire, instead of retiring to easier circumstances, as some men might do, he came back to his native province where he has rendered distinguished service to his country through his public activities and public service.
Doctor Murray has been the president of Saskatchewan university since its inception and has a knowledge of Canada not excelled by anyone. He was a Gilchrist scholar and a professor of repute. To these gentlemen we entrusted the inquiry as outlined by order in council dated November 20, 1931. May I for a moment direct attention to what they did? I am going to read extensively from their report-although such a practice is sometimes burdensome-in an effort to bring it to the attention of the Canadian people. They reported:
In the course of our investigations we have held eighteen sittings, occupying fifty days altogether, and have travelled over most of the main line mileage of the two chief railway systems. Throughout our journeys we were accompanied by the responsible officials of both railways, thus enjoying the advantage of almost constant discussion with them of matters relating to the inquiry, and of transportation problems more particularly affecting the territories traversed. Our itinerary included the principal centres of the various provinces, with the exception of Prince Edward Island, the only province of Canada in which railway competition may be said to be non-existant. In the ease of Prince Edward Island the provincial government kindly indicated their willingness to transmit in writing any representations on the general question of transportation they might desire to make. With this exception we have had the benefit of direct conference with the government of each province, which has included, in most instances, a full statement by the provincial prime minister of any considerations of a special or local character affecting the subject 
of our inquiry. The expositions we have received in this way of provincial policy regarding highway construction and motor traffic have been comprehensive and valuable.
At all of the provincial capitals visited, and also at Vancouver, Calgary, Montreal and Saint John, we have conducted, in addition, public hearings, duly advertised, at which representations from public bodies, labour and transport organizations and private individuals were invited and received. A list of witnesses appearing, and of persons or organizations who have filed submissions, is included as an appendix to our report.
I shall content myself with laying this foundation, before I proceed to make reference to the findings of the commission, by saying to this house that I believe no commission more competent has ever been appointed in this country to make such an investigation. I do not believe the language of that statement is extravagant, nor is the fact important that they were appointed by the previous government. That statement is based upon the personnel of the commission, upon their industry and their desire in and concern for all that affected the welfare of this country as related to the problem of transportation.
I know that when the report was published there was a great deal of misapprehension on the part of many people, because I think I should say frankly to this house that an effort has been made to have it appear that from the day the late government took office until the last day it held office it was opposed to the Canadian National Railways. But those who will take the trouble to read the reports on the subject and the statutes of this country will realize that the Canadian National Railways came into being by virtue of the efforts made by the Union government under Sir Robert Borden, through the bill then submitted; and under and by virtue of the powers conferred by that bill upon the governor in council the final proclamation was made that merged into one system the Canadian Northern, in its various ramifications and interests, the Grand Trank Pacific, the National Transcontinental and other lines. That proclamation was made by virtue of a statute which was piloted through the house of that day largely by Mr. Meighen. When it is said that this party or the late government was opposed to the Canadian National Railways I should like the country to understand that during a long period of five years, over sixty months of untiring effort to maintain its integrity, to provide money to pay its deficits and to enable it to function, during those long years the constant endeavour of the then government was, not to destroy but to maintain the system, not to lessen but to

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
improve its efficiency. But unfortunately- and I say unfortunately with very great deliberation-there was a school of thought in this country that believed that when you have to deal with a problem that vitally affects the very life of the country, if you can play politics with it, so much the better. In the west the Free Press constantly made the people believe that the approach of the government was an approach to destroy and not to support the system. The opposition of that day, now the government of the day, constantly tried to make it appear that the then government was endeavouring to destroy the road. Well, I can only say that, earnest and anxious as I am that the road should succeed to-day, under the control and direction if you will, as the minister says, of his government, even greater was the desire in those days that it should succeed. Why? Because unless it can succeed this country cannot maintain its solvency as a nation. Every thoughtful man in Canada knows that that is so, and this commission that dealt with it and found the facts upon which it predicated its recommendations realized as business men, as railway men, as security holders, as men interested in the maintenance of the credit of the country and of the railways, that unless some action were taken danger of a most grievous kind confronted us and might indeed lead to disaster. That is the reason I desire, with great effort, to refrain from making a political address this afternoon and to place on Hansard extracts from the report of that commission, in order that those who take the trouble to read what the minister has said or what is said by others in this house may realize that in the minds of the members of this commission the situation was dangerous, if not fraught with immediately possible disaster, and that action of the most drastic sort should be taken if we were to preserve the railway system as such and the credit and integrity of the country.
There was one thing the minister did not do this afternoon, and I shall anticipate it before I deal with the matter as it is referred to in this report. He did not deal with the fact that the difficulties to which reference had been made could be solved by taking up the rails and abandoning thousands of miles of railway. That is where politics comes in. Leaving out, if you will responsibility for the construction of the rails, there was the recommendation of the removal of rails and the abandonment of lines; and every time there was the slightest suggestion that anything of the kind was contemplated my friends opposite cried to high heaven that the people must be protected and that these
lines must not be abandoned. That is but natural. The minister has not nor have I the power to lift the discussion entirely out of politics; it has been too closely connected with politics for twenty-five years. What was onoe the proud boast .of a party has now become a dragging legacy that threatens the very life of the country; and when suggestions are made that there should be an abandonment of mileage, the party in opposition during the last five years expressed of course, upon the hustings and elsewhere, strong views on the problem; and I suppose that if the government of to-day undertakes to abandon lines it is expected that the opposition shall oppose that view.
Is it any wonder that we have a railway problem of this magnitude or that it will increase and finally end in disaster if we approach it as the minister did this afternoon in the early part of his address? I am going to refer to some of these paragraphs, because after perusing them the other day I realized that the people of this country had not any clear appreciation of the problem. If the hon. gentleman opposite speaks a little louder I shall be able to hear him; if he desires audibly to interrupt he might speak more moderately. I desire to point out that the early part of the report is but a resume of the history of transportation in Canada in the early days. It requires nothing to be said except to indicate the vast sums expended on canals. I quote from paragraph 9:
9.	The promise of railway construction formed an integral part not only of the confederation of 1867, but also of the terms upon which Prince Edward Island and British Columbia later entered the dominion. The obligation to the maritime provinces was discharged by building entirely at public cost, the Intercolonial Railway from Halifax, N.S. to the St. Lawrence at Riviere du Loup, by the construction of the Prince Edward Island Railway, and the provision of a train ferry between that island and the mainland.
10.	The agreement to connect British Columbia with eastern Canada by a railway from the Pacific ocean was fulfilled by the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Failing to interest private capital in this project the government undertook the work as a public enterprise. Later a syndicate, which afterwards developed into the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, entered into an arrangement with the government to construct this transcontinental line in ten years, from 1880 to 1890. The agreement provided that the country subsidize the company by a gift of twenty-five million dollars, twenty-five millions acres of land, and of the railway lines already constructed with public moneys at a cost exceeding thirty-seven million dollars.
11.	The company carried through its undertaking in five years in place of ten, during which time the government paid the Canadian
C.N.R.[DOT]-Board oj Directors

Pacific $10,189,521 for 6,793,000 acres of land relinquished by the company, and guaranteed securities of the company to an amount of $15,000,000 to assist its finances over a diflicult period. The company paid the guaranteed bonds upon maturity, and the country was relieved from the responsibility of the guarantee.
12.	Eighteen years after the completion of the Canadian Pacific, parliament (in 1903) authorized the building of the National Transcontinental Railway from Winnipeg, Manitoba, to Moncton, New Brunswick, as a part of the Grand Trunk Pacific project. In 1911, the construction of the Hudson Bay Railway was undertaken, also as a government enterprise.
The three railways, the Intercolonial (including the Prince Edward Island line), the National Transcontinental, and the Hudson Bay. embodying 4,650 miles, constructed exclusively, with public moneys, have been operated by or on behalf of the government of Canada. While prior to 1917 the Intercolonial in certain years paid operating expenses, the three railways have earned nothing by way of interest upon the total investment, which, together with certain deficits on operation, now total $512,000,000.
Then comes the beginning of western railway construction.
Some years after completion of the Canadian Pacific Railway, construction was commenced as a private enterprise, upon a line of railway running from Winnipeg in a northwesterly direction, with Edmonton as its objective, and easterly to Port Arthur, Ontario. This line came to be known as the Canadian Northern Railway. It secured substantial cash subsidies, guarantees and land grants from the dominion parliament, provincial legislatures and from municipalities. By 1901, the line had been completed easterly to Port Arthur; and by 1905, westerly to Edmonton, Alberta.
This was the first of the lines extended ultimately to the coast. Parliament did not authorize the extension of the Canadian Northern to Vancouver; that was done through legislation enacted by the province of British Columbia. But parliament did subsidize the construction of the Canadian Northern railway to the summit of Alberta, where it connected with the Canadian Northern in British Columbia.
Proceeding with paragraph 14:
In 1903, the Grand Trunk Railway, which had been operating for over fifty years in Ontario and Quebec, and owned direct lines from Ontario through the states of Michigan and Illinois to Chicago, determined to extend its lines to the Pacific coast of Canada. They made application to the federal government for a charter to construct the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast, and to make connection from eastern Canada to Winnipeg through the United States by way of the company's Chicago lines, and by securing running rights over United States railways to the border of Manitoba.
The application was refused, but an alternative arrangement -was proposed by the govern-

ment which contemplated the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast, with an eastern connection to be provided through a publicly-owned (National Transcontinental) line from Winnipeg to Moncton, N.B., via the city of Quebec.
If, in 1903, the Grand Trunk Railway Company in the east, and the Canadian Northern Railway Company in the west, had been told they must come together and constitute a Becond transcontinental line, the country would not have been called upon to face the present gravely alarming situation, while a powerful corporation, with a serviceable railway from ocean to ocean, owned and operated by private capital, would, with the Canadian Pacific and Intercolonial, have given the needed transportation facilities for the present and reasonable future requirements of Canada.
The ultimate decision of parliament led to two transcontinental railways being constructed in addition to the already established Canadian Pacific Railway.
That is the record of the commission. We must take it as we find it: it cannot possibly, I think, be controverted. Then we had, of course, these lines uncompleted when the war began in 1914. You will recall the efforts made to rehabilitate them by loans and by guarantees, and possibly to save them from receivership. In my place in the house I supported a receivership and opposed the government of the day. I believed that the proper course to pursue was to place those lines in the hands of a receiver. The leaders of the government I supported at that time thought otherwise, but that did not deter me from placing on record my views of the situation, and I voted on that matter against the government.
Having taken the action that was taken to preserve those companies and save them from receivership, the next step was to appoint a commission to make an investigation as to what should be done with the properties. Without going into it at length, it is sufficient to say that in the end all those properties were merged into what is known as the Canadian National system: the Canadian Northern Railway, with all its subsidiary companies and branch lines and affiliates; the Grand Trunk, with its properties in the United States; the Grand Trunk Western, with the Central Vermont, the line running to Portland, the new National Transcontinental from Winnipeg to Moncton, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk Pacific branch lines, the branch lines in Alberta and in Saskatchewan-'both of which provinces, together with Manitoba, have made commitments by way of guarantee or otherwise which, of course, it is impossible for them to pay, and at the present time such guarantees are paid out of the federal treasury. That was the position with respect to them when the order in council was passed

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
under the authority of the legislation passed by the government of that day. We thus have a single system of railways that did not come into being as a system, but came into being because of economic and financial conditions that necessitated, in the opinion of the government of the day, their being united as one system. That of course makes it impossible to compare this system with the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian Pacific developed as a considered whole. The Canadian Pacific was developed as a railway; its branch line system was considered as such with relation to the whole. It deliberated over every action that it took and every extension that it made was in the light of its general plan. But that is not so in the system with which we are now dealing. The system which came into being under this order in council was a combination of many systems, many companies and several roads, in two countries at least, some und r provincial and some under federal control, and not devised or developed as a unified system, but developed along three lines and ultimately merged into one. That is the reason it has been so difficult to deal with, and that is the reason why, notwithstanding the speech made by the minister at Toronto' and at Three Rivers, I think that before he achieves the end he has in mind, unless he is prepared to adopt some of the drastic provisions of this report, he will indeed be as old as Methuselah.
I wish to deal here with one observation made by the minister. He referred to the fact that the chairman, in his evidence last year before the standing committee, alluded to a letter which he had received from me, and that was given as some reason why steps had not been taken to deal with the capital structure of the national railways. I trust that the hon. gentleman, before making that statement, took the trouble to look at the record, because the other day he himself referred to the fact that the whole case of the Canadian National Railways was sub judice because of a case now before the privy council. Therefore he must have known when he dragged that into the debate that it was being done for no useful purpose but rather to indicate that there had been an interference with the authority of the members of the commission by the government of the day. Such of course is not the case. The truth is this, that Mr. Lovibond, one of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway, owning a small number of shares of each type, has taken steps in the courts to have it declared that the legislation that resulted in the removal of the names of the Grand Trunk shareholders from their registers in Dashwood House and the substitution of the name of the Minister of Finance as the holder of the shares was beyond the competence of this parliament to enact. That matter was argued a few weeks ago before the privy council, and the argument took many days.
I understand that Mr. Lovibond has now said that he is prepared to accept damages rather than a return of the status quo, and that the whole question may involve the launching of a new action, or whatever it may be; but the final determination of the question as to whether or not we are validly in possession of the property has not yet been made by the courts. I did say then, and I said to the chairman, as I say to every member of this house, that I did not believe that any government with a sense of responsibility would permit any changes to be made in the capital structure of a railway when it was not yet determined whether they legally owned it or not. That was the reason steps were not taken to deal with the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. It is sufficient now merely to refer to that, because I proceed to direct attention to what the findings of this commission were. At paragraph 28 you have a summary:
Government ownership of railways on a large scale as a national policy was not contemplated or planned by any government and was not submitted for adoption to the people of Canada. But when in 1917, the government refused to permit the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to negotiate for the majority shares of the Canadian Northern, there was practically no escape from government ownership of all the railways now comprised within the Canadian National Railway system. The consequent completion and operation of the hitherto privately owned and operated lines with the publicly owned railways followed as a matter of course. Thus by a combination of contractual obligations and parliamentary measures, the country was projected into the railway business on a large scale.
That, in a single paragraph, summarizes the situation. The Canadian people were not called upon to make, by plebiscite or otherwise, a declaration as to their views with respect to this matter; the administration and ownership of these properties by government came about in the manner indicated by the report.
I think I can shortly summarize the findings of the commission with regard to the period from 1923 to 1931 by stating that after the arbitration had been completed as to the value of a certain class of Grand Trunk shares, resulting in the arbitrators declaring, with a dissenting judgment, that they had no value, the case subsequently was appealed to the privy council which sustained the opinion of the majority. While awaiting that final
C.N.R.-Board of Directors

determination the properties at times were administered jointly, when it became apparent that they were no longer able to provide for their necessities by their own resources. Perhaps in order that those who read may have this shortly before them, I should refer to two of the paragraphs:
Following upon the consolidation of many lines into the Canadian National system, in 1923, the railway has been energetically administered, and has deservedly won approval by its success in welding together the various forces of the separate companies in the consolidated system.
Running through its administrative practices, however, has been the red thread of extravagance. The disciplinary check upon undue expenditure, inherent in private corporations because of their limited financial resources, has not been in evidence. Requisitions of the management have been endorsed by governments, and successive parliaments have voted money freely, if not lavishly.
Within the railway organization there has been freedom in expenditure and encouragement in plans for expansion and extension of services which were inconsistent with prudent administrative practice. The administration failed to realize that this country, with the greatest railway mileage in the world in relation to population, could not afford further capital and maintenance expenditures for unwarranted branch lines, for de luxe services, for unrequired hotels, for the building of ships in competitive service to be shortly abandoned; and, generally, for costly adventures in competitive railways out of proportion to the needs of the country.
There is a statement that has aroused the animosity of some of those who supported the present government when it was in opposition. But, sir, if any man in this chamber will be fair and merely take the figures as to expenditures, as they were produced and shown, he cannot but agree that this is a correct and sound conclusion on the part of these commissioners. In private conversation I have heard no one dispute that, but naturally in this house one hears entirely different views. Then section 35 of the report expresses a thought that I believe must be in the minds of many:
There has been in the country a general sense of expectancy that the publicly owned enterprise should give all and sundry the railway service desired, and there is no evidence that the' representatives of the people in parliament exercised any appreciable restraint upon railway estimates placed before them.
Well, Mr. Speaker, how could you expect it? After all, members of parliament are human; they are thinking of their constituencies and of their party fortunes, and their desire to project a branch line here and a branch line there, to extend further this line or that line, and this attitude reflects the inevitable disaster that overtakes parliamentary effort to deal with a property owned by 
the people themselves. This is beginning again now, as I am going to point out presently. The minister, who has not been here during all these years, understands it only from having read it. Alas, many of us know it from another angle altogether; we have seen it. When I say that a few months ago money was standing in a bank representing the sale of guaranteed securities to construct a line from Calgary to Edmonton, part of the grade of which had been constructed, the minister will understand just what I mean. That line probably never will be built; I do not think it will, but there you have an illustration of what is meant by this report, in dealing with this problem. How are we to get out of it? How are we to get beyond it? How is this country to save itself if we continue to play politics with the Canadian National railway system? I ask you that, Mr. Speaker, and presently I am going to point out what has happened since October 23, to show that we are just going back to the thin red thread of extravagance and worse, to complete subjugation of this great property to political considerations and control.
This is not a matter of party. I wish I could speak as with the tongues of angels and convince my fellow members here that we are trustees of a situation so grave, so difficult and so far-reaching, the consequences of which must be carried by those yet unborn. I wish I could convince hon. members that we must approach this problem not from the angle indicated by the minister in the first part of his speech but from an angle that far transcends any mere miserable party consideration, in the earnest hope and desire of lifting it out of the morass in which it now finds itself by reason, as I shall say, of a lack of support being given the earnest effort that was made to lift the matter out of politics. That is the real reason.
I do not propose to-day to deal with the financial side of the question; I am not going to further harrass an already harrassed people by pointing out to them how great are their responsibilities financially and how large is the measure of their obligation. That can be done by others in this chamber; I merely wish to point out that they are so vast that the mere contemplation of them is calculated to fill any reasonable man with at least alarm, shall I say.
The reason I took some little time to refer to the personnel of the commission was because in his speech the minister said that anyone who would make one of the recommendations made by the commission was lacking in common sense. I cannot think he meant it in that way, but that was what

he said. I am prepared to compare the minister and his common sense with that of the commission, and I think the Canadian people would be prepared to do so also. Why he should indulge in such an extravagant statement I do not know, but he thought it necessary to do so for some purpose, and I desire to make my observation in that regard quickly as I proceed because, as I say, I am not going to deal with the enormous financial obligations involved, except in the broadest and most general way. But if hon. gentlemen will take the trouble to ascertain just how much per minute it has cost this country since we became the owner of these railways, and what has been the inevitable result, they will then have a clearer appreciation and understanding of the problem. I do not say so much per day, so much per month or so much per year, but just so much per minute, so much per sixty seconds. That, I think, should afford hon. gentlemen a clearer appreciation of what is involved.
The question of what has been put into these properties is dealt with in paragraph 37 of the report:
It will be observed that the dominion treasury has expended on or furnished to these publicly owned railway properties cash amounting to one billion two hundred and one millions of dollars ($1,201,000,000) exclusive of the Hudson Bay railway.
That was in 1931. It will be remembered that when the report was presented it indicated that we should no longer issue and guarantee railway securities to capitalize deficits but that the nation itself should bear the deficit incurred. It will be remembered also that in the statute this provision was included. If hon. gentlemen are interested in that provision it will be found in section 12, which provides that-
Income deficits shall not be funded. Amounts provided by parliament to meet capital expenditures shall not be diverted to cover deficits in operation unless with the express authority of parliament.
But the important words are "income deficits shall not be funded." So that under the law as it now stands we have since 1933, that is during the years 1934 and 1935, been providing for the capital expenditures of the system and for its deficits as a part of the debt of the Dominion of Canada, recalling that in 1931, exclusive of the Hudson Bay railway, to which reference will presently be made, we had $1,201,000,000 invested in cash in these three properties, and the deficits that have been incurred since have been added to the nation's debt, because they may not be funded as they were during part of the previous period. For instance, if the railway
C.N.R.-Board of Directors
