required $100,000,000 the dominion guaranteed securities and they were sold, part of the proceeds being used to pay deficits and part used for additions to rolling stock and equipment, roadbed and so on. I will not do more than take a few words of summary from the Duff report, section 42:
Net income available for interest and dividends is the significant factor in the economic life of a railway system. In the case of the two Canadian railways there has been a marked fall in net income in the years since 1928. That the true picture may appear, figures are appended for the nine year period, 1923 to 1931 inclusice. These show in separate columns tlie net earnings from railway operations after taxes have been met, the net income receivable after charges for hire of equipment, joint agreements, et cetera, have been met, and, finally, the interest demands.
Now, there is a misunderstanding that I find on the part of many with whom I discuss these matters as to the relation of gross to net earnings. When my friends pick up a newspaper and find that the gross earnings of the Canadian Pacific or Canadian National have been so many dollars for the week and the net earnings so much, they think that the difference is left with which to pay interest. The average man on the street thinks that. But it is not. Before a dollar of it may be utilized for that purpose the railways have to pay rent of leased lines, wheelage rights, rent of other properties, rent to car equipment trusts if chargeable to revenue, and all the hundred and one things that enable a system to function. If hon. gentlemen are interested they may turn to the report of the Canadian National Railways for the year ended December 31, 1935, at page 19 of which they will find the following figures:

But let us see what the first charge against that is. It is railway tax accruals. The average man, I repeat, reading these reports in the newspapers, thinks the "net earnings" are available to pay interest, and I have suggested, although I believe it is the custom of the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States in the preliminary reports to treat it just as we do, that it would be well

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
so to make the report that the Canadian people from week to week would realize whether or not the railway had any money left to pay interest or had gone behind after paying what must be paid before there is any money available for interest. The railway tax accruals for 1935 were $5,209,133.04. a little less than in 1934 when they were $5,241,857.95.
Then uncollectable railway revenues. These were in the traffic receipts because they expected to collect the money, but last year the Canadian National was unable to collect $94,037.6il, and the year before $46,813.24. The effect of those and other items was to reduce the net railway operating income of the Canadian National last year to $7,424,121.25 as against $6,324,680.25 in 1934.
But you are not done yet. You add your revenue from hotel operations, and expenses of hotel operation including taxes on hotel properties, and these result in net hotel operating income of $101,770.76. That is a highly commendable result; after paying operating costs, which in the case of a hotel include maintenance of furniture and equipment "in their integrity," I think are the words used by auditors, as well as payment of taxes, the hotels earned last year $101,000, Then we come to such items as separately operated properties, showing a loss, and we reach the figure showing income available for fixed charges as $8,014,635.82 in 1935, which is less than the amount in the year before

$8,616,760.98. But from that there is to be deducted the following items: rent for leased roads, $1,372,712 in 1035 and an almost identical sum in 1934. Then you add amortization of discount on funded debt, that is the charge made each year because securities were sold at a discount. That took over a million dollars. Thus you had a situation develop where you had between five and six million dollars left to pay interest. The interest that had to be paid last year on long term debt was $53,468,792 as against $55,811,745 the year before. But there was also the interest on unfunded debt, which means interest payable to the banks for temporary borrowings, which amounted to $182,125 last year, and $211,058 the year before. So that the net income deficit, before interest on dominion government loans, transferred to profit and loss, amounted last year to the sum of $48,878,181 as against $49,605,719 the year before.
I have taken the trouble to go into that in a little detail because I have friends who are unable to understand why there was a deficit of $48,000,000 on the Canadian National Railways last year, when they pick up reports

in the newspapers from week to week and see that the gross earnings so far exceeded the net earnings. I have given these facts in order to remove any misunderstanding there may be in the minds of those who may take the trouble to read what is being said.
There we have the situation brought down to date, indicating the amount of deficit on the system last year. That is the amount of money, apart from capital expenditures- the income statement only-that had to be found by the Canadian people to pay the interest due to the public, not to the government. I am told by many people that it would be manifestly unfair to deal with the moneys due the government, because that represents capital invested by the Canadian people in the road, and unless a dividend is paid on it they must be prepared to accept the loss as part of the incidence of public ownership. The argument is not unfair. But leaving that entirely out of the question., there remains the interest that has accrued on securities held in Great Britain, in the United States, in Canada, in almost every country in the world; held by insurance companies, by trustees, by private investors, by banks, by almost every type of investor in the world. Last year to pay the interest on these securities $48,000,000 was required of the Canadian people. Obviously they could not bear that burden of taxation, and so we went on the markets of the world and borrowed the money with which to pay it. The Minister of Finance the other day referred to what he had to do because on the thirty-first of December last it was necessary to make adjustments in dealing with this matter. There is the situation that has accrued to the Canadian people by reason of the venture in which they embarked.
The amount due in connection with maritime freight rates I have left out of this discussion, because I have left out entirely what are called the eastern lines.
I shall not take time this afternoon to analyze the capital expenditures made, but I recall that many years ago, when I voted against the government of which I was a supporter and said that to make the Canadian Northern of any value would require an expenditure of one hundred million dollars, I was jeered at for putting at so high a figure what was required to rehabilitate that road and make it part of our transportation system. I shall hot do more this afternoon than to direct the attention of the people to what is said in the report as to expenditures on capital and how large these capital expenditures have been made both for the construction of branch

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
lines and for the improvement of the main lines.
So far as branch line construction is concerned any man living in western Canada knows how strongly the people urged that immediate action should be taken to provide them with facilities for sending their grain to market, and we have all endeavoured to do something along that line. The government in 1929 brought out a great plan of branch line construction to which reference is made in the Duff commission report, and the Canadian Pacific followed that comprehensive plan of branch line construction, involving, as is pointed out in paragraph 50 of the report, the construction of 4,161 miles of road and the buying of 857 miles, the major portion of which, according to paragraph 53, was in the western provinces, and at a cost per mile, according to the same paragraph, much larger than it had been believed would be necessary for the purpose. I am not going to do more than read paragraphs 58 and 59:
58.	To sum up, it is clear that there was intense rivalry between the two systems in new territory, particularly in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. The construction program of one company was responded to by an equal or greater program of construction of the other. The development of this territory did not meet expectations, and the railways now find themselves with additional traffic mileage and an increased burden of capital charge.
59.	It would be fruitless at this stage to apportion the blame for the competition in branch line construction, but there is no doubt as to the disastrous effects of this competition, and it is imperative that conditions be imposed that will make impossible a repetition of the rivalry in the extension of railway mileage that marked the period from 1923 to 1931.
In the bill before us there is no provision of that kind. In the first days of this first session of 'a new parliament there has been nothing suggested of that kind in the declared policy of the administration. I take it that inasmuch as the authorization of branch lines will not be given, therefore the necessity for it is not so great.
Then I come to the acquisition of branch lines by purchase. I am not going to indict, as I readily might, the former Liberal administration, now the government, for the cost of those lines. There is not a member of this house who does not believe they cost more than they should, and who does not know that some of them are not worth anything like the amount that was paid for them. I leave that entirely out of the question and point out that the railways taken over by the government prior to 1918 cost $9,559,686, and from 1918 to 1920, $6,641,659.
Those are the particulars given on page 22 of the cost and rehabilitation of the railways taken over by the government.
The report proceeds to give the purchases by the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways of other lines, divided into separate classes. Then it deals with the cost of hotels. It says:
63.	The Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways own twenty hotels and twelve summer resorts, and are financially interested in a number of other hotels and pleasure resorts. In the ease of the Canadian National the hotels and resorts are operated as part of the railway organization; in the case of the Canadian Pacific they are separate organizations.
64.	The Canadian National hotel investment, at December 31, 1931, amounted to $31,828,234, and the Canadian Pacific, $71,148,772, a total of $102,977,006.
65.	The following statements show the total investment in hotels at December 31, 1922, and also the investment at December 31, 1931. It will be seen from this statement that the Canadian National increased its investment in hotels during that period by 229 per cent and that the Canadian Pacific increased its investment by 193 per cent.
I shall only say with respect to hotels that they never have themselves been profitable adjuncts to railroads. In a broad and general way they are supposed to assist in the adjustment and maintenance of traffic, and railways have accordingly engaged in their construction and in their purchase and operation, but in some countries the view has been held that that should no longer prevail and that railways should not be permitted to operate and maintain hotels. At the moment I express no opinion on the subject, except to point out the enormous sum that has been expended in railway hotels, which is referred to in paragraph 67:
67. An analysis of investments in hotels reflects similar results from competitive conditions to those which prevailed between the two railways in the larger sphere of operations, with practically similar results-the Canadian National steadily increasing its investment despite increasing losses, and the Canadian Pacific adding to its investment to an even greater extent than its competitor, without commensurate return on the investment.
One point as to competition which I think the people of this country should keep before them is this, which is stated in paragraph 69 of the report:
69. The Canadian Pacific has stated that in no ease has that company bnilt an hotel in any city where an hotel had already been erected by its competitor. This cannot be said of the Canadian National, but, in fairness to that company, it should be mentioned that their hotel at Winnipeg was constructed in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific venture, and taken over with that property.

The foregoing does not take into account other legislation which provided for the refunding of $18,000,000 of maturing securities, nor $6,396,000 voted for the Hudson Bay railway and terminal development, in the same year.
152.	The net increase in funded debt of the Canadian National due the public for the year 1929 amounted to $144,670,459; whereas the annual increase for the previous six years had averaged $28,897,648.
153.	Annual interest on the funded debt in the hands of the public, which, at the end of the year 1928, was $41,810,880, increased to $55,587,145 at the end of the year 1931, due largely to the expansion policies of 1929.
I was going to put the figures on for last year but they are now well known to the house.
Under those circumstances I think every hon. member will agree that the government was warranted in taking some steps to endeavour at least to give effect to the report of a commission of that calibre, which investigated the matter as thoroughly as I have indicated.

speechtext: In what year and what month was that statement made by Sir Henry Thornton and Sir Edward Beatty which the hon. gentleman has quoted?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Those two statements
were made to the commission itself in 1931

during the progress of the investigation. The commission then dealt with the contributory causes of the railway problem, dealing with excess mileage, which I think must give every member of the house pause-why? Because we all find it difficult to bring our minds to the conclusion that we can agree to the lessening of railway mileages in the communities we represent. Shortly put, that is the position. This is the way in which it is dealt with:
156. In the earlier part of this report emphasis has been laid on the excess mileage of Canadian railways. The policy of branch line expansion in the period 1924 to 1930 has also been dealt with. It has been pointed out that the population per mile of steam railways in the United States is more than double that in the dominion, and competent railway authorities in the United States concede that there is a great excess of mileage in their country. Reference has been made to the low traffic densities prevailing upon the greater part of the Canadian mileage. The traffic density maps, which accompany this report, tell the story in graphic form. In the interests of sound railway practice, a careful examination of all light traffic lines should be undertaken forthwith by both railways to determine what should be retained and what should be abandoned. Where the decision is for abandonment, operations should be promptly suspended, and the salvaged material recovered then or later. Thought should be given to the operation of a considerable mileage during a portion of the year only. Radical reductions, not only in the service on these light traffic lines, but also in the mileage of this group is essential if economic security is to be restored to the railways.
Various estimates have been made as to the number of miles involved. Some have gone so far as to say that to carry out that report in terms of the recommendation would involve the abandonment of 4,000 miles. Has any member contemplated what that means? Can it be accomplished by hon. gentlemen opposite? Does the minister say for a single moment that he can accomplish that? That is the question. Just look at that in the light of the figures which were given as to the number of miles of road we have in this country as compared with other countries. Some hon. members will recall the figures. I passed them by, but perhaps I should read them now:

At present it may be said that the mileage is nearer 57,500. These are the figures. Let us think of it and ask ourselves whether we can effectively deal with this problem in the manner which the minister has indicated. Having regard to the speech made by the minister in Toronto, I was awaiting with great interest the enunciation of the government's program with respect to railways. After his highly inspiring observations at Three Rivers I waited with greater interest and anxiety. It all gets down to this, however: We will substitute directors for trustees and having done that we will provide for a nearer approach to parliament and all will be well. I have no desire to discourage the optimism of any new statesman; on the contrary I desire to do everything in my power to encourage him in his laudable ambitions. But although some recommendations of this commission may be lacking in common sense, as he suggests, I believe he will find that their review of the facts is warranted not only by observation but by experience of at least two of them in dealing with colossal problems in countries other than our own.
May I go further now, leaving that for a moment, to look at the remedies suggested. It was not a popular thing to introduce the legislation of 1931. It was realized that our political opponents would seize upon it for the purpose of arousing the animosities of the employees of the railways. And how successfully they did so. No wonder my hon. friend laughs! I have no quarrel with those who were appealed to in the way in which the railway employees were. Their response was certainly effective, and it was immediate. I daresay the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) recalls the observations made by the steward in the dining car on wnich he was travelling west. I mention this just to let him know that I knew about it.

He was in Calgary, working with the Canadian Pacific Railway, when he was taken by Mackenzie and Mann as master mechanic, and he has risen to a position of importance. But it is m.y duty to say this, that, temperamentally, he cannot resist pressure. He cannot, in that sense, say no. The pressure of politicians, members of this house, members of the government, is such that he cannot resist it; that is the pressure, not of the opposition, but of the powers that be. I say that with the best intentions in the world, and I say it because I know whereof I speak.

No trustee shall he removed from office, nor suffer any reduction in salary, during the term for which he is appointed, unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.
It must be taken, of course, that this measure is practically removing the chairman from office, and the reasons assigned are such that he has not yet had an opportunity to answer them.

The minister very properly points out that it does not follow that they will be permanent appointees, and I quite agree with what he says. But I point out that he was quite content to give them the powers of all the harbour boards throughout Canada, and three is the number provided for in that bill, so three cannot be such a bad number after all.
Now let us go further. We had that period of time in which to endeavour to secure these men. The commission recommended that we should secure a certain type of men, and we endeavoured to do so. If we are to have full time men the minister will find it very difficult to get men of this type to leave their present businesses and devote themselves to the interests of the railway for any compensation that we may be ready to offer, and now you have taught them this lesson, that an act of parliament does not mean anything; that a man -who has a position may be removed at the caprice of any government with sufficient majority to do so. There is no certainty of tenure whatever; yet you expect the best men of this country to devote themselves to this job. I may say that from the Atlantic to the Pacific we canvassed every section; we endeavoured to induce men, possibly through a sense of public duty, to undertake this responsibility, but they all had businesses of their own. Take a man who is general manager of a great enterprise; what time has he to give to the railway? We 12739-141i
did secure what the minister describes as a company director, but I think if the minister will look at the traffic that the company in which that man is interested supplies to the railway, my hon. friend will realize how disinterested that man has been, serving without compensation, how willing he has been and how earnest have been his efforts to seek some solution for the problems before us. Starting at the Atlantic and going to the Pacific we asked this business man and that, pointing out the public duty and responsibility, but they were not prepared to undertake the work, and this bill was one of the reasons they gave.
Finally Judge Fullerton was asked to undertake this duty. First of all he had a good legal training and had been on the bench for fifteen years. He had acquired a considerable business experience while he was at the bar and, beyond all that, as chairman of the railway commission he had an intimate knowledge of the operations of the railways. I am not dealing at the present time with the human factor, because from the moment he was appointed he was subjected to attacks by the then opposition; from the moment he was appointed he was being held up as being unfit for his job; from the moment he was appointed those who now ask for the support of the Canadian public were loudest in denouncing him as being unfit for the position which he assumed. In such circumstances how could you expect to get results? How can you expect to get results under the bill which is now before the house, if as soon as the names of these men are announced we begin to point out that this man has a drag here and the other has a drag there; that this man has a pull here and he desires this for this or that purpose? You cannot appoint men to positions of great responsibility and say: Behold, they hold great wealth or administer great properties, as one reason why they should be fit for the job. The position of chairman of this board of directors is one of the greatest difficulty, involving the possession of qualities which very few men have, and knowledge which is possessed by still fewer men. These men now are, mark you, not trustees with a certainty of tenure but directors appointed by the governor in council, which is by the government of the day, politically, if you like, knowing that those who hold allegiance to the government and those who support the government must come to them demanding this, that and the other thing. Are these men going to be able to administer this system

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
bo fearlessly, impartially and effectively as to ensure an equilibrium between income and expenditure? Does the minister really think that is possible? Does he think for a moment, with the experience he has had, that it can possibly be so? All you have to do is to realize what is meant by the letter I have read or the other matters to which I have referred and you will have no difficulty in appreciating the situation as it exists.
I am sorry to say that, in the light of the minister's speeches at Toronto and Three Rivers, I do not think he realizes what those forces are to which the commission referred. I do not mean that a member of parliament is going to take the minister by the throat. That is not the point. I have in mind what the report said as to the terrible effect of what is described as the pressure of communities, the pressure of circumstances, if you like. Let me put this to the minister: Does he believe, for instance, that a board of directors will be as able to withstand pressure for the construction of the Montreal terminal-I use that as an illustration because it is not likely to be done-as would a board of trustees? I saw what took place in this house, you see. Does the minister think a board of trustees would have yielded to pressure with regard to the Halifax hotel? Does he think a board of trustees would have done what was done by a board of directors with respect to the Vancouver hotel? Does the house recall the appointment of Mr. Fife-Smith of Vancouver as a director of the Canadian National Railways, and the reasons given by the minister from that province for that appointment? These are some of the factors which ar.e influencing my mind in trying to arrive at a sound conclusion, for I am as interested in this problem as any man in this community, even as much as the minister himself, and in trying to see that what we do shall not bring disaster upon us. What Sir Henry Thornton said about political pressure cannot be denied by any observing man. What Sir Edward Beatty said is equally true, and who of us, reading the history of hydro in Ontario during recent months, can overlook the fact that "politically minded" is a proper description of those responsible for administration?
What I fear, I say to the minister frankly, and what I think everyone fears is, on the part of those entrusted with responsibility at head office, a state of mind, unconscious if you like, that expresses itself in a desire to please those who are in office. How many executives have sufficient strength of character and of decision to take an opposite attitude to that taken by the government? I recall what took place in connection with the
JMr. Bennett.]
Montreal terminal. If I had time to tell this house the whole story in that regard I am sure the minister would understand just what I mean. Consider the National Transcontinental; how did that come into being, and why? No one suggests for a moment that it was ever built to meet a national necessity.

speechtext:
I am sorry that it does not shorten the path of the hon. gentleman to an understanding of the situation, but that had nothing to do with the undertaking. We all know the story in that connection; everyone knows it. Then there was the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific to Prince Rupert, paralleling the existing facilities between Edmonton and Winnipeg, and we know how that came about. There was the projection of the Canadian Pacific, throwing its line in before the Grand Trunk Pacific could be built, by the extension of the old Canadian Northern Edmonton line from Wetaskiwin down to Winnipeg. Knowing all these things one cannot but realize that today we are being asked to make possible the exercise of that unconscious influence, if you like to call it that, upon the executives controlling the situation at head office which will result in politically minded action. Does anyone, for instance, say that the purchase of the Southern Counties railway was that high type of business that commends itself to the experienced and trained executive? Does anyone suggest that the Gaspe and Oriental was of such transcendent use to this country as a supplier of traffic that it was necessary in a business way to acquire it on the terms we did? Hon. members know the reports as to values. Some of those old branch lines served little communities in the east, we understand, but when you get into the other field you cannot for a moment say that it was other than considerations, not necessarily party, but political in their character, which brought about the result.
What we are asked to do now is to perpetuate that sort of thing. I think the hon. gentleman at one time would have been quite well satisfied, unless rumour does him a great injustice, if the present chairman would have resigned, to appoint another chairman and another board, and been content with the board of trustees. But the chairman felt that he could not resign, so we are to have seven directors.
I go a step further. On capital expenditure can you have any greater safeguard than we have now? Is it realized that this house has to vote every dollar of capital which is spent? Will it do anything more under this

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
bill? This house has a discretion to exercise now; it will have none greater under the new bill. If it is intended that the government shall project itself more intimately into the administration then, that is the very thing which the commission said should not be done. If not, the control of parliament is complete at the moment, because nothing can be paid for deficits or capital expenditure or anything that this parliament does not approve; this must be done by appropriation. The board as it stands to-day has not a dollar to spend for capital purposes unless we give it to it; it has not any money to meet deficits except as we provide it. We must provide capital, whether it be for locomotives or cars or rails or roadbed, and under the new bill that will still be so.
You are going to have seven men meeting together, and the will of the majority prevails. The reason the chairman has a casting vote, was such would sometimes be necessary in order to carry any measure. The assumption was that the chairman would have such a sense of responsibility that political considerations would in no way govern. I can speak feelingly; I have been accustomed all my life to write to railway executives, whether of the Canadian Pacific or the Calgary and Eastern or other roads, when I was interested in some man who had met with a hardship. I have done this all my life; I never thought of it in any political sense; I did it both when I was in the house and when I was out, perhaps more when I was out than in. But if I wrote to the chairman of the Canadian National with respect to any matter Judge Fullerton would not for a moment consider it; in fact he charged it as political interference because I suggested it.
And when the minister talks about the two railways coordinating their efforts before the trustee board came into being, I can only say that this is true. In 1931, before the board was appointed at all, I sent a letter to both the president of the Canadian Pacific and the then president of the Canadian National asking them to cooperate in view of the serious conditions in which we lived and the financial obligations we were under. That is no new thing, successive governments have done it. But where in this bill have we any assurance that the evils which this commission fearlessly pointed out are not going to recur? If a board of directors under the conditions to which this commission refers dealt with this property in the manner indicated and brought about
the results that have been expressed, then we know if we know anything that the appointment of another board of directors will bring about the same results. The minister says that the question is one of personnel. So it is, but no personnel that you can get in this country, unless you pay them more than we are prepared to offer them, will leave their present positions for the purpose of serving this railroad. Take the United States; take the history of their railroads; take the salaries they pay. Hon. members know perfectly well we cannot get these men. You cannot get the president of a bank or of a great organization to leave his organization and come and serve the railway. And we know if he gives it part time he gives just such time as he can afford having regard to his other duties. A day and an hour are fixed when they shall meet together. They meet together. They carry out-what? The will more or less of the president, just as this .commission pointed out. That is all. Look at their expenditures: The hotel in Jamaica, these three steamships I have mentioned. Take the Montreal terminals, the hotel at Vancouver, the hotel at Saskatoon, the hotel at Halifax, every one of them; you can just put your finger on it and say: That is the reason. That is the report of the commission; that is what they found. There is their decision. I think no one would question that these men had no personal object to serve; in fact, if anything, they were more friendly disposed than otherwise with respect to the matters with which they had to deal.
I say to the minister that he has not made out a case. The only case he has made this afternoon is that in his opinion the chairman has not done his duty and is unfit for his position. But instead of taking action under section 7 and indicting him so that he would have a chance to be heard, he removes him, although the statute requires that he remain for a period of time. He gives him no opportunity to be heard, except before the special committee, and substitutes directors for trustees although the report of the commission is that under the service of directors, whether under a Conservative or a Liberal government, there was faulty administration and the red thread of extravagance running through the whole of the operations. And, more, there is the effect of politics, exercised not individually with respect to individual persons, but by the pressure of circumstances, of communities, of members of parliament en masse for the purpose of promoting their own political fortunes, and human nature being

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock-I had intended to conclude before that hour-I was asking the minister what he hoped to do by this legislation that could not be accomplished under the existing statute. I thought it well to point out in that regard1 what the commission had to say in their proposals and remedies, commencing at paragraph 195 of the report. They referred1 to the necessity for disregarding such amalgamation, long lease of the property as well as short leases of fifteen years and over. Paragraph 203 reads:
Three trustees should be appointed by the governor in council, in whom should be vested all the powers of the present board of directors of the Canadian National Railways, both in respect of the parent and all subsidiary corporations of the system; and any and every power and authority necessary to enable them to administer the property and operate the system and every part thereof.

C.N.R.-Board o] Directors
I put this to the house: In the face of a finding such as that to which I have referred, can it be said that this house as it is now constituted is better able to recommend an adequate remedy than were those commissioners? Does the minister with his limited experience in dealing with this problem suggest that at this very short date he is so well qualified himself as to be able to speak with more authority than are those men who gave so much time and trouble to dealing with the problem? In regard to the appointment of the trustees, I mentioned this afternoon that the government of the day had full appreciation of the value of the report in connection with the type of men who should be appointed. The report recommends that all should be persons of proved business skill and capacity. I think most will admit that Mr. Morrow is a man of proven business ability and capacity. Mr. Labelle had had considerable experience, not so much in the practise of his profession as in dealing with business transactions for one very important client whom he represented in Montreal. He brought to bear upon the problems that he had to consider a trained mind not unaccustomed to dealing with business problems of the greatest magnitude. In the case of Mr. Morrow, as I say, I think his capacity is known to all those who have any knowledge of the business of this country.
I have mentioned already the considerations that brought about the appointment of Judge Fullerton. I should mention that it was regarded as absolutely essential that there should be some measure of continuity in management between the outgoing board1 and the new trustees. Both Mr. Morrow and Mr. Labelle had been on the board and they were continued so that continuity might be maintained. For the life of me I oannot understand just what difference there is between the suggested proposals and those embodied in the statute itself. Paragraphs 205 and 206 of the report provide that the budget requirements of the system are to be made known. These paragraphs read:
The annual budget of the railway should be under the control of the trustees. Amounts required for income deficits, including interest on railway obligations, for capital and for refunding, should first be submitted to the treasury board for its approval and presentation to parliament by the Minister of Finance.
Since the debt of the system in the hands of the public is now very large and more than the railway can carry from its earnings even under improved conditions, sums which are required to meet deficits should be voted by parliament annually and not raised by the issue of railway securities as has been done in recent years. This recommendation does not apply to capital for improvements and betterments nor to amounts required for refunding.
These recommendations are embodied in the report and it is somewhat difficult to understand what will be the difference between the new board of directors considering the situation and making recommendations as to what is required for capital, for other purposes and for the deficit, and the present board of directors, which now considers these very problems, making recommendations as provided for by the statute. According to the provisions of the statute parliament deals with the matter and provides the money and the week before last we voted substantial sums to the railway for that purpose. There is now standing on tihe order paper a bill which contemplates the voting of a potential deficit before it is known. All of this is a negation of tihe principles that governed in connection with this matter, under either the report of the commissioners or the provisions of the statute itself.
With relation to the chief operating officer, I confess I was unable to follow the minister. The statute distinctly and positively states that the operating officer shall have to do with the operation of the road, the administration in the broad sense being entrusted to the chairman and the trustees. If, as has been said, the chairman segregated certain activities; for instance, if he said that he would undertake to be the executive officer with respect to hotels or with respect to the law department, tihe fact remains that the president was responsible for the operating. I cannot see that that division of duties could in any sense lessen or limit the field. For example, it is well known that the vicepresident in charge of traffic may have certain obligations. It is well known that the vice-president in charge of accounting may have certain obligations and the chairman of the law department may have to do with certain other phases. If, as chief officer of the road, the chief executive or the chairman says, "I am willing to undertake responsibilities that link executive action to administrative action in connection with several activities," to which reference was made this afternoon, I can only point out that as a result of his efforts, he brought about surpluses where there had been deficits. I think the minister mentioned this afternoon a surplus in connection with hotels, and in connection with the steamship lines the same condition prevailed. Of course, the law department is not a revenue producing department, but one would expect that a former justice of the Supreme Court of Manitoba would be well qualified to assist in the administration of problems which had to do with law. Therefore I find it difficult to understand why the

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
attack was made in the form in which it was, unless the minister understood the chairman to indicate that he regarded himself as the chief operating officer of the railway. The statute says that he is not and the recommendation of the commissioners in that regard has been followed. As I say, I find it difficult to understand what is meant by that attack.
With respect to cooperation, I stated this afternoon that the commissioners recommended the closest cooperation. In paragraphs 210 and 211 of the report they embodied this recommendation in terms which have found expression in the statute itself. I say once more to the minister that there can be no useful cooperation if there are two considerations always before one or both of the parties cooperating. There can be no such thing as real cooperation if each is waiting for the other one to suggest that there shall be the taking up of lines on his road or on the other man's road. These considerations must be overcome by mutual understanding that there may be lines taken up on both roads.
Lastly, and more important, is the second consideration. Last fall I heard appeals being made to the railway employees that amalgamation or unification might involve a possible loss to some of them. This afternoon the minister talked about human relations between the president of the road, who had worked up to that position from the mechanical department, and the employees. Is it proposed that because someone suggests that some proposal may have a temporary effect upon someone, the Canadian taxpayer is to be taxed forever? Is that what the minister means? The facts would certainly indicate that that is so.
Someone pointed out that the roundhouse in Ottawa was in a disreputable condition, was no longer capable of serving the purpose for which it was constructed. It was pointed out also that across the bridge there could be found in Hull a recently completed roundhouse owned by the other road and quite capable of meeting the requirements of both. If meaning is to be given to the words of the minister, it will be extremely doubtful, because of attention having been directed to what might result with respect to the employment of some people, whether an effort will be made to bring about the ultimate use of the Hull roundhouse when the Ottawa roundhouse falls into obsolescence. I want to make it perfectly clear that I think it would be far better for the people who are

employed to be employed by a solvent system, by a system not in the hands of a receiver, than by one no longer able to maintain its services efficiently and effectively. In other words, more people will ultimately be engaged in more stable and certain employment if there is a realization that there should be cooperation between the two railways. I think it is axiomatic that this must be done to secure efficiency on the part of both. If, in the approach to cooperation, there is a combination of the two qualities or factors which I have mentioned, the inevitable result will follow that there will be no cooperation under this board, for the simple and obvious reason that if there is the haunting spectre of a political result following at the end of administrative action, the inevitable consequence will be a continuance of the very conditions which we have in this country. How could Judge Fullerton function, with the conditions prevailing which have been made apparent to this house, neither road willing to move its tracks, each waiting for the other to suggest that the other man's track? should be moved, and with the realization that there is more trackage than this country can possibly support, as is admitted by every one? In that condition of things, how is the change from trustees to directors going to effect an improvement in the situation? For the responsibility of the government, of the country and of the taxpayer has not been changed one tittle from the recommendations of the commission as embodied in the act. They were stated in somewhat different terms, and that is all that can be said.
A point to which the minister did not direct attention and which I had thought would be in his mind is this: This system of railways has been made up out of not one but many systems. May I read paragraph 84 of the report:
Representations have been made with respect to the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. This problem presents several aspects. One is the very large number of companies whose corporate existence must be maintained. Another is the large number of different bond issues and mortgages with different rates of interest, expiring at different periods and with all sorts of different clauses in them. It has been stated that included in the National Railway system there are 251 different bond issues and mortgages; that there are 80 different issues of certificates in the hands of the public; that there are 139 companies whose corporate existence must be maintained; and that 42 separate income accounts and 90 separate balance sheets have to be prepared each year.

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
Obviously the suggested changes are not going to improve that situation, and so far as capital structure is concerned, no change except by parliamentary action can in any sense deal with that condition. Therefore, so far as that outstanding point is concerned- and we have met it by the appointment of trustees-much will have to be undone that has been done and in the end there will be no progress in that direction. I point this out, because it has its effect upon the situation as a whole.
Then there is a third point, the last one which I desire to discuss in this connection. It must be within the knowledge of the house that when parliament declared that there should be no more funding of deficits it meant that the Canadian taxpayer had to find the money and that thereafter there would be no charge for interest appearing in the Canadian National report. So that the report for 1934 and the report for 1935 do not disclose the real condition, because the interest upon the deficit for 1934 and 1935 is being paid by the country as part of the national debt. Those who are interested will find, at page 19, that in 1935 the interest due the public on long-term debt was $53,468,792.22, whereas in the preceding year it was $55,811,745.85. There has been an economy effected by refunding operations carried on by the government. The interest upon the deficit of 1934 is now part of the national debt of Canada, and the interest on the deficit for 1935 is also a part of that debt. The appointment of directors cannot improve or change that condition unless the government is prepared to capitalize against the railways the deficits from year to year. I would point out further that last year we had to find over $48,000,000, which, added to the income available for interest of over $8,000,000, made the payment on interest account the sum of $56,000,000. That is a very large sum of money.
I wonder whether the members of this house realize that it represents over $1.75 a second. Do they realize that when I speak of something over a million a week it is a large sum of money? Few men have taken the trouble to reduce it to the smallest unit of time. But when I point out that while we sit here, as every second goes by, there has to be provided from some source, either from traffic or from the Canadian people by taxation or by means of an addition to their debt, about $1.75 a second, the house will appreciate the astonishing sum of money which is charged against the people.
During the last few years, especially since 1931, my friends opposite were content to
endeavour to throw discredit upon the administration of the railways, to assert that the party in power at that time was anxious to bring about the destruction of the system, whereas in point of fact, day and night, we were labouring to provide the wherewithal to maintain its integrity and solvency from the standpoint of those who held its securities. And in that we succeeded. Hereafter fair minds, those who are able to take a less prejudicial view, will realize that the task we undertook and discharged successfully was a great and difficult one. During the election, it is quite true, as the minister has stated, that the government said they proposed to change this condition. They did undoubtedly so state to the Canadian people; they did state to them thiat the government of that day was responsible for the condition which had been brought about and that it was intent upon the destruction of the Canadian National system. I can only reiterate that, as the records in that regard indicate, such was not the case; they speak for themselves. It will be found that the appeal which was successfully made to the railway men of the country, the appeal which secured their support in overwhelming numbers for the government now in power, was based upon a wholly inaccurate appreciation of the difficulties of the problem and an unreal understanding of just what was involved. There is no government in any country at any time that is not concerned about employment being made possible for every man within the borders of that country. Every government desires that. But when one is faced with a situation such as we have here; when the statute itself declares that neither amalgamation nor unification was intended or proposed or possible until parliament should speak; when one finds further that the mere suggestion that there should be a lessening of expenditure in connection with express and telegraph systems raised in this house such a cry against the administration of the day, such an upheaval of prejudice and an appeal to the public against the taking of any action, does the minister say that he does not intend now to take action; that he does not propose in any sense to give effect to at least three of the suggestions of these coordinating committees of the two roads? Is there to be some unification of action with respect to express and telegraph services? Are rents to be paid every year for two places where one might suffice? Does this mean to say that while provision is made for these things they shall not be carried into effect lest, peradventure, some
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

man will find his interest temporarily affected? It must not be forgotten that when the very suggestion was made with respect to these two matters that had been dealt with by the two systems carefully, with much detail and over long period's of time, the result was as I have indicated.
There is still another point to which attention might be directed. So far as my memory serves me, wherever there was a suggestion that certain roadbed be abandoned there went up the cry that this was an effort on the part of the government of the day to destroy the system. One piece of road a few miles in length has been successfully abandoned. The rest of them have not been so treated, although the two roads were of the opinion that some action of that kind might be taken. I do not know to what extent they arrived at conclusions as to total mileage that might be dealt with, but this I do say, that unless the Canadian people are told frankly that there can be no carrying into effect of the recommendations made by the commission; that that cannot be done, they must continue to pay and pay and pay. If it were a question only of paying one would not be so vitally concerned, but there is a limit to the powers of the Canadian people to pay. There is a limit to the power of taxation against our people, and that limit has been reached. If one is not familiar with the history of taxation in other countries; if one does not realize wbat eleven million people scattered over half the continent are able to bear, one may continue to say: Pay, pay, pay. But the obligation is a direct one. It is imposed upon the people; it must be paid by the taxpayer in the form of interest upon increased securities issued by the country itself and not by the railroad. Unless this commission is entirely mistaken; unless we are so remarkable a people that rules which govern other countries have no application to us; unless it be true that one Canadian can produce as much traffic as two people in the country to the south of us; unless it be true that we are able to operate our railroads more cheaply than any other country, unless it be true-and we have a climate which makes this impossible-that we can operate the railway on a ratio of gross income to operating costs more easily and better than any other country, then of course this legislation can have no purpose and can effect no good. All it means is that you have drawn nearer and nearer politics and business^ business administration and .political action; that you are that much closer to the demand that clean, frank, honest administration shall be the creature of political considerations and not

of business rules and principles. These things are brought nearer and nearer by the legislation which is before us.
I do not know to what extent the members of this house can respond to what they conceive to be a national crisis. I do not believe for a single moment that this country has reached the limit of its powers of expansion or development. But I know that we have provided in this country facilities for a population nearly if not fully twice as great as the present one, much larger, in fact, than that. And our transportation system is threatened by the bus on the one hand and the aeroplane on the other. The number of passengers being carried by air from some of the great western cities to the south of us to the Pacific coast shows a very large increase. I know that the other day four extra planes, carrying twelve passengers apiece, went from one city to the Pacific coast. On the other hand we have the bus system and all these are the products of the internal combustion engine. Yet to-day, notwithstanding the condition that confronts us, one may hear men demand air-cooled trains, stream-lined trains, increased facilities of various kinds, regardless of cost. I wonder whether the minister thinks for a single moment that to put these powers into the hands of these seven men is going to change these conditions for the better. I think not.
I can only say this, that having induced the Canadian people to believe that the late government was the enemy of the Canadian National system, although through the stress and strain of the greatest depression the world has known that government, with great difficulty, maintained the system in its integrity; having succeeded in creating a public opinion hostile to the government of the day on the part of the employees of the roads because they feared that if certain action was taken they would find themselves for the moment with less employment; having succeeded in doing these things, the government now finds that the responsibility rests with it to promulgate a policy. That policy, after all this careful1 consideration on the part of the minister, consists in the substitution of seven directors for three trustees, and no real change in any other feature, so far as governmental action or control is concerned, except that implied in the statement made the other day by the Prime Minister as to what the effect of this bill was in providing an opportunity to exert power and pressure upon the administration of the road to secure the ends of particular individuals. Apart from that, this bill does not contemplate any change that I can see, anything that makes for the benefit of the road or

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
for lessening the burden upon the taxpayer. That policy will not solve our railway problems. That suggestion will not in the end help the employees. It will still leave fixed charges to be met. It will still leave the Minister of Finance to worry, as did his predecessors in office, amid stress and strain to find the money with which to meet the continuing deficits of a system which now has fixed charges of upwards of twenty million dollars greater than they were in the glorious days of what was assumed to be prosperity.
It is all right for Mr. Fairweather, at Moncton, to enlarge upon what he says can be accomplished with a gross income of so many dollars and a net income of so much. All I can say is that until there is a clear realization of the obligation of parliament to deal with this problem as one of business and not of politics, there can be no clear-cut solution. It has not come to-day. After listening to the speech of the minister I say that it has not come by this legislation. It will not come until Canadians of all classes, in every walk of life, and of all political faiths, have a clear understanding of what is involved, for with the people themselves rests ultimately the remedy. As long as they are content, without a clear appreciation and understanding of this matter, to keep on making new and fresh demands upon governments for new money, for fresh capital, for better facilities, for improved trains, and for better pay. there will be no solution of this problem. Those who sit to the left of the Speaker and know something of this matter, having been through it, who know the anxiety which attends the maintenance of the system, who understand all too well that man is but a fallible creature and that as long as he desires to promote his own interests in the political sphere he is not very likely, whether he be Liberal or Conservative, to devote too much of his time to a consideration of the fundamental questions themselves, realize that there will come a time, as in every country there has come a time, when the problem will become so acute, the danger so imminent, the risk so great that men will bestir themselves, forget their personal animosities and political difficulties, and rally to a common cause to save from disaster that which they cherish and love. I believe, judging from the resolution which has been produced here to-day, that that day has not come, but some day it will come, and when it does, those who now sit to the left of the Speaker will be found ready and prepared to make such sacrifices as may be demanded for the salvation of the country and the saving of the taxpayer from ultimate ruin.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I will trespass upon the patience
of the house for but a few minutes while I express my regret at the character of the bill, now under consideration, purporting to be a solution of the railway problem of Canada. I do not intend to indulge in recriminations or to stir up the mess that was made some twenty years ago in connection with this railway question, a mess so odorous that it stinks to high heaven. Both parties have to bear a share of the blame; if one overbuilt, the other overbought, and the regret is that in recent years no serious attempt has been made by any party to solve what is to-day the most perplexing and most important subject before the Canadian people, a question upon the solution of which depends the credit and, I venture to say, the solvency of this country.
Now let me cite a few figures to show the serious depths to which we have fallen in the mismanagement of this problem. In 1935 the total cash deficit of the Canadian National Railways exceeded $47,000,000 and the net loss on the system, as set forth in the report, amounted to more than $115,000,000. The debt of the road is $2,809,000,000. If a proper business policy, one that commended itself to men of sense, had been adopted in 1921 when the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific got into difficulties; if these roads had been put upon the auction block and had been taken over by their creditors, more than one billion dollars of the debt of this dominion would have been avoided and no impairment of railway service would have occurred,, because wherever roads were necessary they would have been continued in operation by the new proprietors. When the railways were formed into the Canadian National system the total debt was $1,336,000,000. In 1933 the total debt was $2,745,000,000, an increase of $1,409,000,000 in the short period of thirteen years. Since then, that is to say in 1934 and 1935, a further sum of a little more than $200,000,000 has been added to the capital debt. The cumulative deficits of the Canadian National railways between 1923 and 1933 amount to $663,000,000 including interest on loans from the government, or to $303,000,000 exclusive of that interest.
I ask hon. gentlemen: How long can this country continue to meet these deficits without imposing a taxation repressive of trade, and thereby hampering the rehabilitation that we all hope is in the not too distant future? The bill before the house is not even skin deep. You, sir, may remember the story of
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

Mrs. Partington, as related by that eminent wit, scholar and essayist, the Reverend Sydney Smith. Mrs. Partington was an elderly lady who occupied a humble cottage on the seashore. One day a violent storm came up, causing a tidal wave. The tide approached closer and closer to Mrs. Partington's house whereupon the old lady, who was of a resolute, determined character, rushed to her kitchen, seized a broom and came out and fought the incoming tide. The battle went on, but needless to say poor Mrs. Partington was vanquished and had to give up the contest. The bill before the house will be no more effective in meeting the rising tide of debt and taxation occasioned by Canadian National railway deficits than was Mrs. Partington's broom against that tidal wave.
We sometimes hear of a reconstruction of the capital account of the railway. I have heard in this house and I have read in the newspapers proposals that the capital structure should be written down. What nonsense I You could write it down to one dollar and you would not save a penny of taxation for the people of Canada. Why? Because that is a debt of the dominion government, represented either by bonds issued directly by the government or by bonds guaranteed by the government. To transfer that debt to dominion account from railway account would not lessen the burden upon the people by one iota, but this is what it would do: It would make the position of the railways very much more precarious, because without any interest charges our western friends, and our eastern friends too, for that matter, would sing out for a reduction in rates because of the apparent surplus, and even the employees of the company would begin an agitation for higher wages.
I have always thought that only by some process of unification or amalgamation shall we ever escape from the dilemma which faces us. But I realize that this house, and apparently the electors of Canada, are set against a course of that kind. What then remains? Cooperation with a view to economy. It is true, as the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has said, that the railway men of this country did not show confidence in the Conservative candidates in the last election. I think it fair to say that perhaps ninety per cent of the railway employees of Canada are supporters of the present government. Why? Because of their fear that the Conservative party is inclined to a policy of amalgamation. My contention is that by cooperation, if you will, the cost of operation can be gradually and in increas-

ing ratio every year reduced without a single employee in any department of either railway suffering. That economy will be brought about in two ways, by old mortality-Death- and by the pension bill. There will be an increasing number of present employees who every year will disappear by one or other of these means. In that way, with reduced mileage one can in the course of a very few years bring the numerical strength of the railway staff to a parity with the operating needs of the railway.
I was glad to hear the minister intimate that Mr. Hungerford of the Canadian National Railways will probably be chairman of the new board of directors. The leader of the opposition had a complimentary word to say for Mr. Hungerford, though he feared that he lacked back-bone, the ability to say no, a weakness with which I most cordially sympathize, which I attribute to the kindness of his heart. Of his ability as a railway executive there can be no manner of doubt. The late Sir Donald Mann a few years ago told me that in his opinion-and he had some knowledge of railways-Mr. Hungerford is the equal of any executive operating manager on the continent of America. Knowing him as I do, having the high opinion of him that I have, I am extremely glad to learn that he is to be chairman of the board of directors.
