speechtext:
But I regret that I cannot pay the same compliment to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) who entered public life with a very high reputation for business ability, and with wide experience, and was elevated to one of the most important positions in the government, when he comes to this house with so feeble a measure as the bill before us to cope with so great and momentous a question. He does not do himself justice. He lacks the courage that I expected from him, and allows "I dare not" to wait upon "I would." None the less we shall never get anywhere in the solution of this question by skirting round the circumference of it. We have to get to the core, to apply drastic remedies. In no other way is it possible to avoid what I think it no exaggeration to say is almost impending disaster.
I have spoken on the point that the railway employees have nothing to fear. I have referred to the absurdity of the suggestion that by cutting down the capital account of the railway a surplus can be made to appear.
I would say this to the minister:	Is there
not some lack of consistency in his policy by

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
land and his policy by sea? He found when he came into office a number of harbour boards upon which were local businessmen, familiar with the needs of the particular ports in which they were residing. He wiped them out and named three gentlemen who are to reside in Ottawa to manage these ports. But when it comes to the railway it is somewhat different; he wants more or less local, certainly sectional direction, and not a commission. I think there is some element of inconsistency there.
But, after all, that is a small matter. What I w'ould plead for is this-and I wish I had more force with which to do it-that this house should apprise itself of, should realize, as the Minister of Finance well does, the seriousness of the situation with which this country is faced in connection with the Canadian National Railways, and that we should shed our party politics. Now, in this first session of a new parliament, is the time in which we should have drastic legislation.. Wait a year or two and it will be too late. At least let the government insist-it is going to take the power through this board of directors-upon serious and drastic cooperative steps with a view of reducing these dreadful deficits with which we are faced. Something can be done. And remember this, that to-day if you deprive a community of a nun-profitable railway line, the situation is not as it would have been fifteen or twenty years ago when there were no motor cars or motor buses or motor trucks. These are competitive forces that are playing the very mischief with the earnings of the railways to-day, and they are here to remain. So it should be borne in mind, when this question of closing down non-profitable branch lines is under consideration, that communities will not suffer by their closing. Remember, too, that the whole is still greater than the part, and if it becomes necessary for the treasury of Canada to hold out a helping hand to a larger number of people or to continue the present assistance for a yet longer time, its ability to do so will be materially increased by measures of drastic economy in connection with the Canadian National Ralways.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you are familiar with the French saying, "Ne reveillez pas le chat qui dort," or as we say in English "Let sleeping dogs lie." I have not taken much part in the debates of this house or occupied much of its time since the beginning of this session, and now I have just a word to say in reply to what was said by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) this afternoon. He mentioned me by name and
praised me for being frank in acknowledging that I recommended some men for shovelling snow along the track of the Canadian National railway. Well, sir, I do not know if that is an offence mentioned in the criminal code of Canada, but here are the facts.
Last winter snow fell in more abundance than in, previous years, and a great many men were to be hired on extra gangs by the Canadian National Railways to shovel snow. A great many of them wrote to me here, asking me to give them recommendations. I started to do so, but the number was so large that finally I aked some friends of mine to form a committee for the purpose of giving the work to those who most needed it, as the right hon. gentleman has been fair enough to say. It was not a pork barrel matter at all. It was simply a question of giving help to those who most needed it. This committee, which was composed of prominent citizens in my home town, has done excellent work in classifying according to their needs those who wanted work at shovelling snow. They were classified as, first, supporters of families; second, married men without families; third, boys who were supporting families; and fourth, unmarried boys. That was a fair classification, and in fact the town has been most satisfied with the arrangement because less money has been paid out in unemployment relief while these men have been shovelling snow along the track of the railway. I mention this not by way of excuse or justification but simply in explanation of what happened. My political correspondence is an open book, a big book possibly, but I have nothing to hide in it, and I am very much surprised that the right hon. leader of the opposition did not enjoy the same clear conscience when I asked him to produce papers. He refused and said that it was a confidential matter. But I say to him that he can come and look through my files, provided nothing disappears, from A to Z. I have nothing to hide. What I say to him I say to my people, and what I say to them I say here in this house.
I can tell the right hon. leader of the opposition that if my home town of Riviere du Loup has suffered so much for lack of employment in the Canadian National railway shops it is because of the dirty patronage of the Tories when Sir Robert Borden came into power. As the right hon. gentleman has spoken, let me speak in my turn. There was a man now dead who was Postmaster General in Sir Robert Borden's government. I shall not identify him any more plainly than that. He was a Conservative. There was another gentleman here, a Liberal, a lieutenant-governor of the province of Quebec, and in
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

order that there may be no mistake he was not of the privy council at Ottawa. These two gentlemen met together in the early nineties in Quebec and invested a small capital of $5,000 in a company called La Compagnie des Terrains sans Bruit, or The Noiseless Land Company. That important company, with a capital of $5,000, and comprising some of the big men of both parties but who should be disowned and denied by all respectable men of all parties, bought a swamp on the outskirts of Quebec at St. Malo as land for railway shops. There were other prominent Tories with them, and they bought this swamp for $5,000 and tried to sell it to the Liberal government when the Liberals were in power. Sir Wilfrid Laurier refused to agree to this, but as soon as the greedy Tories came into power one of their first deeds was to buy that swamp, for which $5,000 had been paid, for the huge sum, comparatively speaking, of $160,000. Some profit, eh, for a swamp! And then what was done? The Tories built a railway shop on that swamp and called it the St. Malo shops.
After the shop had been built they had to bring down men and machinery, and they brought good men from Temiscouata to work in that shop. They brought machinery from the shops at Riviere du Loup. If any member of the house wants to have more information about the matter he has only to look at the Hansard of the session of 1925, my first session, and he will see enumerated there the number of pieces of machinery, important and expensive machinery, which were transferred under Tory rule from Riviere du Loup to St. Malo, and the number of men who were deported from that beautiful city of Riviere du Loup to that swamp on the outskirts of Quebec at St. Malo. That was done by the Tories. Let them rest in peace-but I wonder about that! That is what was done. It was just for graft, and Tory graft, that these good workingmen of the Canadian government railways were deported from Riviere du Loup to Quebec in order to justify that graft of $150,000. It was done at the expense of my home town of Riviere du Loup. That is what the Tories have done, and I am not surprised that the right hon. leader of the opposition turns crimson. He must be ashamed of what his party has done to my dear home town of Riviere du Loup. That is one thing the Tories have done, one thing which they cannot justify, and those who have wrought damage must make reparation. It seems to me that the government of the day was responsible for that wrong done to my home town of Riviere du Loup. It is up to the government of Canada to repair that wrong. I feel quite at 
home when I complain about the way in which my home town has been treated, and this is the place where I should complain.
There is a lot of hyprocrisy in connection with this matter. We hear it said:	Leave
the Canadian National Railways alone; do not touch it. I hear some so-called important business men say: Do not touch the Canadian National Railways. Does the right hon. gentleman suggest that the people of Canada, who have an interest in this system valued at more than two billion dollars, should not be interested in its operation? If I have an interest in a two million dollar concern and am walking down the road and this concern is on the right, am I to keep my eyes left? Am I to do that when by looking through the windows I can see what is going on? We are 245 members who represent the people of this country, and to whom the people have said: You are to look after the future of this country for the next five years; you are to support a government that will express the views of the people for the better management of this country. You are to be just rubber stamps; you are to give powers of attorney to a certain number of men who will do the business, who will look after the railways and the other business of ithe country and you will not have a word to say about it. A business worth over two billion is worthy of consideration. Are we to give a blank cheque in connection with this? Are the members of parliament to be criticized because they want fair play in connection with the management of the Canadian National Railways, because they want fair play for the men, for the passengers and for the management, even when they do not realize it themselves?
The hon. member for St. Antoine-West-mount (Mr. White), one of the two deans of the house, a gentleman much respected, has said that Mr. Hungerford was weak. One has to communicate with the management of the railways. If I write to the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Howe), asking for information about expenditures in connection with which the railways come here for assistance, I am told I cannot have it. This is the same information as I received last year. There must be a nigger in the woodpile. How is it that I cannot have the information asked for? It is because of the legislation brought down last year and the year before. It would be better if the leader of the opposition did not smile ait that because he will remember that t/he suggestion was made in the house that the Canadian National-Cama-dian Pacific bill should be submitted to the committee on railways in order that the mem-

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
bers of that committee might have an opportunity to examine Mr. Hungerford and Sir Edward Beatty and obtain the information necessary properly to discuss the bill. This request was denied me by the previous Minister of Railways and Canals, Mr. Manion, on the plea that it would be too expensive. After plenty of trouble on the part of an hon. gentleman in the senate, I was able to obtain the information that the cost of summoning witnesses before the senate committee in connection with this bill was the enormous sum of not a single cent. Yet the previous Minister of Railways and Canals was bold enough to say that because of economy he must refuse the members of this house the privilege of asking questions of these witnesses.
When the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Belanger) was asking questions about the tremendous expenditures on strawberry jam, he received no answer. It was absolutely impossible to get an answer to a query about this man Laforce who has done more than anyone else to place settlers upon the rocks in impossible places. We are told that these things are not in the interests of the country. How is it they are not in the interests of the country? We are here to discuss Canadian National business and when we ask for information we should receive it. This information was refused in the past, but we must have it if we are going to correct these things.
We hear a lot about the so-called business men of this country, but I think it is time the truth was told about the millionaires of Canada. Most of them are short-sighted. If the country is in trouble, it is because of the silly experiences of these people. If it has survived, it is not because of the millionaires; it is because of the small traders who have more business acumen than most of these other fellows who have become rich at the expense of the people through watered stock.
These are the facts. From the way in which discussion is being carried on in this house, in the senate and in the press, one would think we are making a political joke of the Canadian National Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway. This is most absurd. If they come here for money, we must know for what that money is intended. If we are to investigate the business of the Canadian National Railways, we must do the same in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is only fair that this be done. The number of men unemployed has been increased enormously because of the increase in unemployment, brought about in the ranks of the employees of the railways by the policies of the last government. When the
bill was discussed in 1932 and 1933 the Liberal members stated very clearly that the best way to bring about a revival of business and prosperity in the country was to bring about a revival of trade. Two years later the then Minister of Railways and Canals and the right hon gentleman who is now leader of the opposition repeated the same thing. They did not realize that it was because of their stupid tariff policies that trade had decreased bringing about a decrease in the income of the railways.
I do not intend to speak at great length about this matter and I rise in order to prevent the house from forgetting about these things. The right hon. gentleman's policy was a complete failure and fiasco, but he is ready to give advice to all-take it or leave it: I am the only one who is right. He takes himself quite seriously. This is most extraordinary as what he should do is to hide himself under his desk. He has not the least sense of responsibility for what has happened during the last five years. No one in this country has forgotten it, but he comes to this House of Commons just as though he had received a mandate from the people in the last elections. Oh, stupendous! Has he no calendar? On the calendar for last year there is one word in particular, and there are two numbers, in flaming letters. There is the month of October and there are the two figures "1," "4"-October 14, the day on which the people of this country passed judgment on the last administration, which was making an effort to survive its period of five years from July 28, 1930, to July 28, 1935. August passed; September passed and two-thirds of October passed before the right hon. gentleman handed over the reins of power to another administration. Think, sir, of the misery, the anxiety and the worries that have been experienced in every house during the last five years. The country was getting weaker and weaker though the voice of the right hon. gentleman was still strong, assuring the people that there was no depression. Most incredible! I do not want to be hard on any one and this speech is most lenient, but we must think of the responsibilities we have here. The right hon. gentleman has his own responsibilities, and they are great, but they are not greater nor are they less than those of any of his colleagues in this house; they are the same. He must therefore face the facts as they are and must not build skyscrapers on the head of a pin, nor can he build skyscrapers on nothingness.
Here are the railways. The Canadian Pacific Railway was favoured, in spite of the fact that it was a private company. Let us

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened most attentively this afternoon and evening to the speeches made in connection with this very important measure, and I realize, with those who have already spoken on the question, the magnitude of the problem that confronts parliament. This is one of the most important matters that parliament has to deal with. May I for a moment or two deal with some of the statements made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe) in this chamber in introducing the measure. I was sorry in a way to note what the minister had to say with respect to the board of trustees; I felt as he was speaking that he was not doing justice either to himself or to this house. Here we have a board of three trustees who, being appointed by parliament, are in a sense employees of this house. Their lips are sealed; they are not in a position to answer the criticism that has been made of them by the minister in charge of the transportation system of this country.
I notice that he pointed out that two of the trustees are members of the legal profession. He inferred that for that reason they were not qualified to deal with matters pertaining to railways. There may be something in the minister's contention; in fact I think that, as a general criticism of lawyers, he may be entirely correct. But I suggest that before he levelled that criticism against the board of trustees he should have looked immediately round him and seen what position he was in. For what do I find? The Minister of Public AVorks (Mr. Cardin), whose [unction is to look after buildings and to erect buildings, is not an architect, an engineer or a builder; he is merely a lawyer. The Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott, Middlesex), is also a lawyer. I wonder what lawyer knows about the work of a post office. Another lawyer, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), is in charge of the defence of this country. According to the same maxim of course he should not be occuying that position; we should have some one who really knows something about military affairs. Then take the Minister of National Health (Mr. Power); I wonder what lawyer knows about health. In the past it has been customary for successive governments to appoint a doctor to the ministry of health, but now we have a lawyer. This all makes me wonder how the Minister of Railways can manage to sit in with all these lawyers and still believe that they are capable of fulfilling functions for which they are not trained. Further, we have another lawyer, as Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley), in charge of a department of the government which deals with [DOT]customs and matters of that kind.

So much to his credit. I was merely suggesting that before the Minister of Railways criticized the board of trustees because it contains a couple of lawyers, he might look round in his own cabinet and see how well lawyers are represented in the present government.
It has been claimed that this problem is probably the greatest that the present parliament has to face. My personal feeling is that the railways are suffering from the same economic depression as is the whole of the rest of the dominion. I do not think there can be a prosperous railway structure while the country as a whole is in a depressed condition. AA'hen this government has solved the economic problems of the time; when it has brought about a condition of prosperity in the country, we shall probably not hear so much about railway deficits as we are hearing at the present time. I do not believe that any economies we may effect can entirely solve the railway problem. The minister, speaking this afternoon, appeared to chide the existing board of trustees because in the eighteen months or two years that they have had charge of the railway transportation systems of this oountry they have not brought about sufficient economies. He and those who succeeded him this afternoon were unable to tell this house how savings were to be effected excepting in one direction, namely through a process of amalgamation or cooperation or pooling of the sendees of the two main transportation systems. That would involve laying off vast numbers of men who are to-day employed by the railways. I contend that the government will not solve this or any other of our national problems by aggravating the unemployment situation. If it is the avowed intention of the government to force upon a new board of directors a method



C.N.R.-Board of Directors
by which there will be greater cooperation between the two railways, the first thing the government should do is to protect the men who will be affected by such a process. It was claimed, I think by an hon. member who spoke a few moments ago, that there would be no further unemployment of railwaymen if we had a greater measure of amalgamation of the two railway systems. He said that the normal mortality among railway employees and the pensioning of older employees would be sufficient to take care of the situation. 1 do not accept that as being a correct analysis. It might hold good if there were no births in this country, but as the older generation passes away there is always a younger generation looking for employment, and if employment in the railway shops is reduced this will prevent the younger people from being absorbed into what are, after all, useful occupations.
The minister also stated that the trades unions of Canada were strongly opposed to the act of 1933. That is perfectly true. Those who represent the railway trades of this dominion object to the continuous tampering with the management of the Canadian National railway system. It is less than two years since we put in the present board of trustees, and now, for no apparent reason, a new board is to be appointed in their place. How in the name of common sense can we expect anything in the way of confidence on the part of the railway men or any one else in the management of the railways if we are going to have these continual changes, without any apparent reason? It has been suggested by the leader of the opposition that if the board of three trustees had retired there might have been no necessity for the introduction of a bill of this kind. I cannot speak as to that, of course, but I do think that if it is the intention of the government to appoint a new board, consisting of seven men, it should be selected in such a manner that there shall be something in the way of permanency for the men who are to be given that new and very responsible position. I suggest to the minister and to the government that, if it be at all possible, the leaders of the various parties in this house should get together and see whether they could not agree among themselves on seven names to be submitted to parliament as the board to take charge of the Canadian National railway system.
It was suggested that the railway employees were opposed to the changes made under the act of 1933. Well, I can speak for some of the railway organizations and I want to say that they are just as much opposed to the changes

being made by the government now. I want to say further that if the government had been as frank in expressing its intentions last October as it is at the present time a good many votes that were cast in favour of the government probably would have been cast against it, because I have personal knowledge of large numbers of men who voted for the Liberal party because they believed that by doing so they were safeguarding to the utmost the entity and integrity of the Canadian National railway system, just as in 1930 vast numbers of employees of the Canadian National system voted for the slogan, "Competition Ever, Amalgamation Never." We are asked to keep this question out of politics. Well, some of us are very anxious indeed to keep the matter out of politics in order to give the Canadian National system a fair opportunity to make good and to give the people of this country the service they have a right to expect from a nationally owned public utility.
In addressing the house this afternoon the minister also spoke of the human element. In 1933, we in this corner moved amendments asking that the employees on the two railways who might suffer as a result of closer cooperation between them should be given that measure of protection which they have a right to expect. If we bring in a similar amendment this year I wonder whether the government will be prepared to afford that protection. In 1933, when we made that proposal, we were glad to receive a large measure of support from members of the Liberal party. I hope we will receive the same measure of support when we propose a similar amendment in connection with this bill.
So far this question of the deficits of the Canadian National seems to have baffled the best brains we have been able to gather together in the Dominion of Canada. Let me refer for a moment to the commission that was appointed in 1932, the Duff commission. On that commission there were gathered together some of the best railway experts it was possible to secure; yet when the report was summarized and analyzed and presented to the house we found that they really had no solution for the problem of transportation in this country, except the solution of economies and cooperation between the two railways. I do not believe that is sufficient to give this dominion what might be called a sound financial structure for the national railway system. It may be said that I am indulging in negative criticism, and I may be asked what we are going to do about the

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
matter. The fact is that the railway problem is not one of our own making; it is something that was created by people of generations gone by, but it is something with which we must presently deal as best we know how. On this railway commission, as was pointed out this afternoon, we had the chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada ; one of the most experienced railway men of the United States; one of the most experienced railway men of Great Britain, and, among others, Sir Joseph Flavelle, who is one of the best known business men in this country. As a matter of fact we had on this commission some of the most hard-boiled business men in Canada, but after they investigated this problem from all angles they were unable to find a real solution. They brought in a report to which I believe the existing board of trustees has been doing its best to give effect, but without avail. It appears to me that, even though economies may be effected here and there, there is at the present time no solution, with the possible exception of the one to which the government is pledged, which is to increase the trade of this country both internally and externally in order that greater revenues may accrue to one or both of our railways.
There is one point which I should like to drive home with all force possible, and that is the question of the men who are employed on these railways. I will protest as forcibly as I can if efforts are made to amalgamate the services of the. two railways unless at the same time provision is made for the men who will be affected. Large numbers of men were affected by the cooperation between the two railways in the Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa services; those men were laid off with very little consideration, though in many cases they had seniority amounting to ten, fifteen or twenty years. I remember when the matter was raised on the floor of this house at that time; the then Minister of Railways said that if it could be shown that any injustice was being done in the way men were being laid off, with no provision being made for them, the government would consider what action should be taken, and the government would be sympathetic to a proposal which would provide compensation to the men thus laid off.
I should like to point out to the minister that men who are laid off as a result of an act of this kind are in a completely different position from those who might be laid off as a result of slackness of work or for similar reasons. Men employed by the railways will lose their jobs because of an act of parliament; they will lose their livelihood because of something done by parliament, and in that 12739-142$
case parliament has a responsibility to the men so affected. Because of that fact we of this group in the last parliament moved certain resolutions which at that time were defeated, but which we hope will receive a more sympathetic reception when the proper time comes.
There is very little more that I wish to say in connection with this bill, though I may have something to add when we are in committee. I hope, however, that when the bill is in the committee stage we shall have a more detailed statement from the minister as to his intentions and those of the government in regard to this matter. He has not told us very much thus far. He said, of course, that the government desired to change the provision concerning the board of trustees because it had not gone far enough in the direction of economies on the Canadian National system and in bringing about a greater measure of cooperation between the two railways. When we are in committee I want that part of the minister's statement amplified to a much greater extent, and I trust that we shall receive a great deal more information than the minister vouchsafed to the house this afternoon.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing for which you can give the late government credit it is the way in which they handled this railway problem. On the second rending of this bill, no doubt, under the rule of anticipation members will be forbidden to deal with the whole railway problem as it should be dealt with in this house; we can deal only with the amendments proposed to the act of 1933, and I have particular reference to the establishment of a tribunal as between the two railways by the 1933 act as it has been amended by the government of the day.
Notwithstanding the pronouncement made by the government and members of the cabinet in the last election and the one hundred and seventy members elected, the action of the government on the railway problem as found in this bill is very unsatisfactory. The government so far refuse to state their policy. As I see it they are going back to the "big I" days of 1921 to 1930, when this tremendously extravagant expenditure such as was never before known in the British empire went on: Hotels, golf courses, useless duplications, needless branch lines and waste. This bill is a going back to t'he old days of the lack of control of parliament over these expenditures. On April 6 last, without any notice from the government, without any mention of the matter even in votes and

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
proceedings, with sixty per cent of the members not present in this chamber, the most important motion of the session was passed, handing, over the head of parliament, to a select committee known as the committee on railways and shipping owned and operated by the government the whole budget of the Canadian National Railways. This railway never was under public ownership. Two railway systems are dealt with in this bill, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific; one is supposed to be publicly owned and the other privately owned, although the privately owned -one received grants, bonuses, subventions and subsidies by cash and land grants and guarantees. The Canadian Is ational was never under public ownership; it was a number of privately owned roads that were not able to succeed and were amalgamated under the Canadian National system. The mistakes of that system were almost entirely due to private ownership. Throughout its whole history the Canadian National was never under public ownership. After it was taken over by the government the first board under Mr. Hanna made a real effort to take the road out of politics and succeeded. Since then two commissions have been appointed and both commissions have recommended something in the way of a tribunal to hold the balance between the two railways.
In 1917 in the days of the Union government parliament had the Drayton-Acworth report. When the Liberal party took office in 1921 they entirely ignored that report. In the first place the railway commission were supposed to be the arbitrators, but they had no control at all. Then the government of that day decided to appoint a sort of star chamber committee known as the committee on railways and shipping, and that committee was substituted for the commission. The minister would rise in the house and nominate the committee and that would be the last heard of the railway problem for the session, parliament handed the problem over to this star chamber committee, whitewash committee I call it, and I attended it many times. I was summoned before the committee once to give some evidence about a national coal policy, and the head of the railway told me that I was proposing an unscientific system of freight rates or lunch counter system of freight rates for coal, and the railway officers opposed that policy for three or four years and then swallowed it. Both these reports recommended some kind of tribunal to coordinate the railways. The management of the Canadian National Railways in 1922 moved the head office from Toronto to Mont-

real, starting off badly, because the old Grand Trunk which formed the best part of the system was a good, solvent railway, and made its money in Ontario. It went into bankruptcy owing to the ''big I's ' of the Liberal party. I assess the blame for the railway situation for fifty years about eighty per cent to the Liberals with their Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern, and twenty per cent to the Conservatives.	_
The government and the Minister of Railways from 1922 to 1930 were never in favour of public ownership. They launched out on a policy of extravagance in the building of branch lines and useless duplications, spending over the head of parliament, more than $590,000,000; wuth interest added it would go away over that amount, parliament having no control whatever of this expenditure. In that connection they violated almost every line of the Drayton-Acworth report which recommended that there should be no building of branch lines or extensions, and no renewal of charter should be granted by parliament until a report had been made to the Minister of Railways by the railway committee and the board of railway commissioners as to whether these branch lines were in the public interest. That policy was ignored and the result was that a great many expenditures were made which should not have been. Matters got into such a bad state that in 1931 the government appointed a royal commission of which the present chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada was the chairman. That Duff commission made a very fine report. I do not know where this country would have been to-day if the late government had not passed in 1933 the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act to implement the Duff report. That proposed some measures of coordination. The commission recommended that the identity of the two systems should be maintained; that the management of the Canadian National should be emanicipated from political interference and community pressure. But we had this body of fifteen men called directors before; it was a little larger in number; one would almost think they were selected as a campaign committee of the Liberal party, a board of directors who did not direct, who knew nothing at all about railways. They were brought here and would meet round the table of this celebrated committee on railways and shipping, where everyone was smoking. They passed the first item and the last and parliament knew nothing about the matter; it was whitewashed in this committee and we could not ask a question about the railways.

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
As to the second recommendation, that the management should be emancipated from political interference and community pressure, under this bill the government is going right back to where things were seven years ago. The third recommendation was that machinery should be provided for cooperation between the two systems for the elimination of duplicate services and facilities and the avoidance of extravagance. One of the best equipped and most honest men appointed on any commission in Canada was F. K. Morrow of Toronto, a brilliant and most popular and gifted young business man who served without salary, and spent almost his entire time in an attempt to carry out that recommendation with great success for the entire system and the taxpayer. The fourth recommendation was the attainment of a scale of economies which would bring the burdens of the national system within reasonable dimensions, and effectively check extravagant and costly operation; and, lastly, there was recommended reasonable protection for the privately owned undertaking against arbitrary action on the part of the publicly owned undertaking, a very wise recommendation. They recommended strongly against amalgamation, and the jurisdiction of this proposed arbitral tribunal and what its powers should be, were set forth very fully, but by the proposed amendments in this Bill No. 21, the powers are going to be vetoed. The old board from 1931 to 1936, tried to run this railway on a commercial basis, but now this board of seven is to be set up to undo the good work. The government should announce who the board are before we pass the bill. We had one "sevenfold amen" commission announced the other day, on unemployment; now we have a second commission, and probably men associated with the big St. James Street interests will make up this tribunal.
I have very little faith in the amendments which this bill proposes. The Duff report goes into the question of the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal. It recommended that it should have jurisdiction in relation to the following matters:
(a)	Joint use of terminals.
(b)	Running rights and joint use of tracks where there are actual or functional duplications, or where such may be avoided.
(c)	Control and prohibition in respect of the construction of new lines and provision of facilities and additional services where no essential need of the public is involved.
(d)	The joint use of facilities where this would promote economy or permit the elimination of duplicating or unremunerative services or facilities.
(e)	Abandonment of lines, services or facilities.	_
(f)	Pooling of any part or parts of freight traffic or of passenger traffic.
(g)	Things necessarily incidental to the above enumerated matters.
There is a wise provision for a tribunal that is to sit and decide on questions of coordination between two railway systems, one privately owned and the other publicly owned. The three gentlemen who composed the board of trustees for four or five years did their utmost and effected a great many economies along the Lines of the Duff recommendations.
I fail to see how this new board can act efficiently if we are to go back to the old order and have politics enter into the administration of the railway. On page 67, in paragraph 226, the Duff commission makes this recommendation:
We feel compelled, as a matter of public duty, to strike a serious note of warning to the people of Canada. Unless the country is prepared to adopt the plan we have proposed, or some other equally effective measures, to secure the efficient and economical working of both railway systems and thereby not only reduce the burden on the federal treasury but improve the financial position of the privately-owned railway, then the only courses that would be left would be either to effect savings in national expenditure in other directions, or to add still further to the burdens under which the industries of the country are suffering by the imposition of yet further taxation. Failing the adoption of one or other of these courses, and there are obvious lijnits to their application, the very stability of the nation's finances and the financial credit of the Canadian Pacific Railway will be threatened, with serious consequences to the people of Canada and to those who have invested their savings in that railway.
But by this bill we ignore the recommendations of the Drayton-Acworth commission of 1917, and the Duff commission of 1931-32, and are going back to the administration we had in the old days, because in my humble opinion you will not be able to keep politics out of the railway. If we are going to elect directors by sections and from classes, the sectional aspect is bound to be looked at instead of the commercial aspect, and you are going to have politics back in the administration of the railway. I was confronted with the same kind of situation when Toronto took over the city's street railway in 1921. We had clamours and agitations from all classes of citizens, from labour and capital, wanting to be represented on the board that was to administer Toronto's transportation system. But we selected a board of three men; by statute their powers were limited, and they were able to administer the city's street railway from the commercial aspect and to effect economies. That is the kind of board we
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

should have to administer our publicly owned road and the privately owned road in this country. If politics had been kept out of the administration of the railway, hundreds of millions of dollars would not have been wasted. The time has come when the Canadian National Railway must be given a chance. It has not had a chance so far. The offices should have remained in the city of Toronto, in Ontario, a public ownership province, instead of being moved to Montreal, because the effect of that was that when the Canadian Pacific Railway wanted to do something the Canadian National from the years 1922 to 1930 used to say: Me too. The failure of the national railway to act in its own interest and in the interest of the public is one of the reasons for the present railway situation.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, in some respects Bill No. 21 ignores the Duff report and the Drayton-Acworth report and puts the administration of the railway back where it was for ten years, when politics entered in. Questions that might well have been taken up by the board were such matters as suburban services, commutation tickets, cheaper fares for weekends and holidays, the problem of the inroads made by bus and motor car competition, but the political directors of the national railway simply stood still and did nothing to meet this competition.
I would like to know what is going to happen to parliamentary institutions in this country when almost every day the government is appointing some commission or another, taking away the powers, prerogatives and privileges of members of this House of Commons and turning them over to a commission. Parliament should be safeguarded against the star chamber secret methods of the committee on railways and shipping. The people have a right to know what is going on in the publicly owned road; they have a right to know how it is being run. Are we again going to allow the management to run up bills of four or five hundred million dollars, as the management did from 1925 to 1930, before parliament can find out anything about the expenditure, and then have us hold a post mortem on it? We have full publicity in some things. The newspapers give great publicity to murder trials, sport and many other things, but most of them at the present time seem to have forgotten that parliament is even sitting. Some of the largest newspapers do not give half a column daily to the proceedings of parliament. I do not know whether we deserve more space or not, but I find page after page of the newspapers devoted to murder trials, sport, and many other things, while, with the exception of
IMr. Church.]
four or five newspapers, hardly a line is devoted to a debate on the deficit of forty or fifty million dollars on the nationally owned road. Few newspapers pay any attention to the sittings here.
I have been very much disappointed with the committee on railways and shipping. Attend one of their meetings and you will see the directors and officials sitting round a table. The committee takes up one item, asks a few questions and then goes on to the next. They might just as well not meet at all. It is nothing but a whitewash. I have attended meetings of the committee for five or six years, and I have never seen the committee conduct its affairs. They let the officials and directors of the road run the whole committee over the head of parliament. We have no control over them whatever. I am absolutely opposed to secret discussions and that sort of committee meetings. It is not Liberalism as I see it. They pass the buck to a committee without any notice of motion. Nobody knows what the policy of the government is on this particular problem or if they favour a merger or not, and the final result will be that the committee on railways and shipping will bring in a report and we shall not be able to ask any questions. What right have the public and members of parliament? Why should the members be ignored in this way? The whole problem will be sent to a committee of this house, and the last state of the Canadian National Railways will be worse than the first.
The heads of the Canadian National Railways in 1924 and 1926 told the railway commission that they had nothing to do with the administration of the railway. They ignored the railway commission and started on a spending bee, the like of which has never been seen in any other country, building golf courses, hotels and branch lines all over Canada under the direction of the " big I," and building hotels extra-territorially. They sold for $50,000 some ships which had cost one or two million dollars and which could have been converted for use in carrying coal from the maritime provinces to the head of the lakes. With a slight change in construction they could have been utilized to carry coal from the head of the lakes to central Canada and from the maritimes to the head of the lakes. Last year 2,800,000 tons of maritime coal were carried to the head of the lakes. Why did they sell these particular boats for such a trifle? The government may have 170 members but the rank and file seem to have no chance at all in this house. Just the other diay three private members asserted the rights and privileges

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
of a member of parliament. If these rights and privileges of private members had been asserted twenty or thirty years ago we would not have had the Grand Trunk Pacific or a third transcontinental known as the Canadian Northern foisted upon the people of this country. This would not have happened if the private members had asserted their rights and privileges and fulfilled the functions which they were sent here to perform. We have got to the same state of affairs where last week three government members rose to criticize a bill to appoint another commission. As I say, if we had had a little more independence in the house, if private members had asserted themselves as being opposed to this secrecy in connection with railway administration, we would not have the spectacle which we have to-day.
There is one thing for which the previous government and the leader of the Conservative party deserve credit. When the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) came into office in 1930 he decided to have a survey made of this problem. For years he had sat in parliament and had seen hundreds of millions of dollars being voted for these railways by the government of the day, from 1921 to 1930, some of which money was being spent without the authority of parliament and without parliament being aware of the expenditure. The result was the Duff report which was presented to parliament in 1932 and which was implemented in 1933 by chapter 33 of the statutes of that year.
The old board of directors in 1926 consisted of fifteen members and the government is now suggesting a board of seven. If the board consisted of only three members it would be closer to the mark. This board proceeded immediately to run the railway in a manner similar to the way in which some of the railways in the United States were being run. A group of the Van Sweringen railways in the United States consisting of the Nickel Plate, the Big Four and the Chesapeake and Ohio recently went into bankruptcy and were bought back for a sum less than $3,000,000. When the head of this Canadian National Railways took office he carried out policies similar to those which had been carried out by these roads by the Van Sweringen brothers. Sir Henry wanted to place 1,000,000 more grain growers into the Peace river district. Parliament knew very little about this, but it objected. Where would we be in these days of depression and reduced traffic on the railways if this had been carried out?
The more I see of this thing, the more I realize that we have no opportunity to deal properly with it. Only the other day this
whole problem was shunted off to a select committee without one word being said or without any notice being given in the votes and proceedings. I have very little faith in the proposed board of directors of seven to be appointed. They are going to have this railroad back to where it was ten years ago- in politics. This board of seven will be merely figureheads because they will know no more about railroads than they do about shipping. We must not blame public ownership for what will happen, as public ownership will have nothing to do with it. That type of ownership has shown what it can do in the municipalities and the provinces and it could show it here if given a chance. But public ownership will have no chance in Ottawa as long as we conduct our affairs the way we do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add a few brief remarks to this debate. First of all, I should like tc direct the attention of the minister and the house to what I consider to be a somewhat important omission in the present bill. It will be recalled that in our Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933, there was a clause inserted to provide for the protection of the employees. Despite the fact that the constitution of the board of management was being changed through the substitution of three trustees for seventeen directors, this was to have no effect upon those who were employed by the road. I shall read the section to make it abundantly clear. Subsection 5 of section 9 of the act of 1933 reads'
Subject to the terms of this act, and until otherwise provided or directed under its authority, every operation and service of national railways shall continue and be continued by all persons now concerned therewith as if this act had not been passed.
The main function of the present bill is in a sense to bring back matters to the status quo, that is, to substitute a board of seven directors for the three trustees. I cannot help feeling that if the subsection I have just read was proper in the act of 1933. it is eminently proper in the bill we are now considering and I cannot understand why it should have been omitted. If it has been omitted through inadvertence, I suggest respectfully to the minister its utility. On the other hand, if it has been omitted in order to remove what would be a restriction upon wholesale political dismissals, then in the interests of the employees of the road I want to deplore this -omission and put myself on record to that effect.
I cannot help being struck by the action of the government in increasing the board of
management from three to seven. If there

Board of Directors

ever was a party that manifested the need of economy in its election campaign, it was the Liberal party. Frankly, I do not see any justification for increasing the board of management to two and a half times its former size. I do not know where the minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Howe) got the idea of doing this, but I am sure that there is one of his colleagues whom he did not consult. I refer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). When reading over the debates leading up to the passage of the act of 1933, I was very much struck with the manner in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce led off for the Liberal party. At that time he used these noble words:
I support the bill for the second reason that the establishment of a small body of trustees of three or four, as the ease may be. will promote efficiency in the conduct of the Canadian National Railways.
Later on, referring to the parliamentary committee on national railways and shipping, of which he was a member, he said:
-we are in favour of a reduction in the number of those who are to form the board of management of the Canadian National Railways.
I would hate to think that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was in favour of a small board when we were in power and doing the appointing, but is in favour of a large board when he and his friends are in that position. I hate to think that, but I do not know what else to think. I have to try to get wdiat comfort I can get out of the statement that the effect of this legislation will be to bring the operations of the railway more closely under the administration of the government of the day. I take it that is one of the functions of the bill, and if it achieves that function I would ask the Minister of Railways to pay some attention to the conditions under which some of the men are now forced to work. I will give a concrete example to show what I mean. In the car shops in my riding-and I fancy this applies to other ridings as well-before cars are repainted they are subjected to a sand blasting process. The old paint is removed by means of sand forced under pressure through a hose. That raises a most dense and suffocating cloud of very fine dust which in the opinion of medical authority tends to bring about the disease known as silicosis. I visited the shops in London to see the process in operation and made careful inquiries, and I must say that it seems to me these men are working under conditions to which they should not be compelled to submit. I found that they were equipped with masks, and I was told

that the masks were the best that science provides at the present time. The main criticism, to my way of thinking, is that although this operation is performed in an enclosed space and not on the outside of a building where all dust is blown away, is done in an enclosed shed, there seems to be no proper draft system. This is something which is of great importance and something which I would direct to the attention of the minister. It is a matter that should be carefully considered before any more refinements and luxuries are introduced into passenger trains. For example, I read in the Mail and Empire of April 13 last this news item:
Air-Conditioning Making Progress Canadian National Railways Announce Plans to Extend Service Dust Is Eliminated
Montreal, April 12.-Good progress is being made with the air-conditioning of equipment for use on the lines of the Canadian National Railways, according to C. W. Johnston, general passenger traffic manager. A number of air-conditioned pullman sleeping cars are now in service between Montreal, Toronto, Windsor, Detroit and Chicago, Mr. Johnston said to-day, and it is expected that the International Limited, and other Canadian National trains on this route will be air-conditioned by June 1st, before the hot summer weather starts. Air-conditioned cars are also in use on several of the other international trains of the company.
I doubt whether there is any class of men -at any rate there are very few classes- who make more use of the sleeping cars on the Canadian National Railways than do the members of this house, and I doubt whether there is any class that likes to sleep in comfort more than do we. But I venture to say that if hon. members could see the conditions which prevail where that sand blasting process is in operation they would say with emphasis that no more money should be spent on luxuries such as air conditioning on pullman cars until that situation is corrected.
I trust-and I should like to put myself on record in this regard-that although the initial act of the government has been to multiply by two and a half the expenses of the board of management of this railway, a real policy of economy will be instituted. It is not pleasant work economizing; it is not popular work, but it is very necessary work. I heard to my amazement on Friday last a statement made in this chamber by a supporter of the government to the effect that the late Sir Henry Thornton was one of the greatest national assets that Canada ever had.
