subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to precipitate myself into this debate at this late hour. I had assumed there might be, from the other side, a defence of the bill introduced by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe), apart from the belated attempt made earlier in the evening with such disastrous effects. The railway problem, as has already been pointed out, is of national importance. The solution that has been suggested by the Minister of Railways in the measure which he introduced this afternoon hardly meets a situation of such gigantic importance. A few years ago there was appointed at the behest of the government then in power a select commission to study the railway problem of Canada and to bring in a series of recommendations on which the government of the day could formulate a policy and proceed to action. I think every member of this house will agree with me when I suggest that the members of that commission were able men who understood their duty and discharged it as commissioners on that occasion. They brought before the government, and ultimately before this house, a report which is worthy of every consideration by every hon. member, and one which should be given very careful study by any hon. gentleman who is at all interested in a solution of this national problem. I do
not think there is a member of this house who does not recognize the magnitude of the problem we are facing. I have before me many articles from which I could quote figures to show the tremendous debt that is being piled up by the Canadian National Railways. The measure that was introduced this afternoon contains in my estimation nothing that will in any way stem the tide towards a greater deficit.
The recommendations brought forward by the present government do not in any way fit in with the recommendations of the commission that was appointed and brought in its report, 1931-32. I cannot see why any government should appoint a commission of able men who go throughout the length and breadth of this country accumulating information, hearing witnesses, getting expert testimony, and filing a report, and then, having received this -report, should put it into the archives merely for reference of future generations of Canadian citizens who may be interested in developing material for debate on some railway problem that may exist only in their own minds. The compilation of this report must have cost the country a tremendous sum of money. It is printed, and no doubt has been in the hands of members since 1932. Yet we find that the present government, having such a report before them, having facts and figures compiled since that report was issued, despite all this wealth of information and experience, come down today with a measure which merely reestablished conditions as they were prior to the inauguration of this special commission to inquire into this national problem. '
The government -that has just gone out of office did their duty as they saw it. They acted on the report of this commission. I am not going to say that those who were appointed and have acted as the three trustees for the Canadian National Railways during the past four years are the best men who could have been secured for their particular positions. No doubt they are men who have faults. But there is no doubt in my mind that the government of the day thoroughly canvassed the situation and did their utmost to secure the best men available at that time.
The only criticism I have to offer of the government of the day in appointing such a trusteeship is that, in my estimation, it was appointed according to a wrong practice. To appoint trustees for a period of years does not commend itself to me, because when there is a change of government, or if those who are appointed are not -acceptable even to the government that appoints them, there they
C.NJt.-Board oj Directors

are, saddled with positions and salaries for a stated length of time, and any government which tries to make those men give up those salaries and appointments has its work cut out; the task is almost if not altogether an impossibility. If any mistake was made by the past government in carrying out the recommendations of the report of the commission, it was that of appointing the trustees for a definite period of time instead of during pleasure.
I read a few days ago a speech delivered in this house by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in which he commented rather vigorously upon such appointments, characterizing them as a restoration of the feudal system as it existed in Europe in days gone by. I quite agree with him in that respect, and I was going to criticize a similar proposal of the minister in another bill he brought in; in fact I handed him an amendment that I was prepared to move, if I had been in the house, in connection with the harbours board, which is to be appointed for a period of years. I do not believe in that kind of appointment, and I believe that in that respect the government of former years made a mistake in connection with -the appointment of these trustees. I believe that if they had been appointed during pleasure we should not now have before us a bill asking for a directorate of seven members. I assume that the government would have taken advantage of the existing legislation and changed the personnel slightly in order to harmonize it with their own line of policy, rather than maintain the present personnel intact. Apparently they are not giving satisfaction either to the government or to the people of this country. In making that statement I do not wish to be misconstrued. I am not criticizing any one individual. But possibly at the present time there are certain members on the board of trustees who can be replaced to advantage, who have not worked in the spirit of the recommendations of this report, a spirit that suggests cooperation between these two great national railways,, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. If such a person is on the board and is not giving effect to that suggestion of cooperation, he has, I thank, been negligent in his duty, and for that reason that person should be removed from that important office. I am not passing judgment; I merely make the suggestion as a possible reason why the government must introduce legislation such as we have under discussion.
It seems to me that the minister must agree that the measure he has introduced is a
I Mr. Walsh.]
retrograde step. I do not believe that to appoint a directorate of seven members will assist in any way in solving the railway problem of Canada. I have not heard him say or any member from the government side suggest exactly in what way this new directorate is going to bring order out of chaos, to stop the piling up of deficits, to do anything that will affect to the advantage of the Canadian people the conditions which exist at the present time in connection with our railways. I wish to read from the report before me the items which suggest the principal contributory causes of Canada's railway situation. Those causes are summed u,p in seven statements. I desire to read them and to ask the Minister of Railways in what respect his solution meets those suggestions. Is any one of the conditions outlined under those items likely to be eliminated as a result of the measure introduced by the minister? I leave it to the judgment of the house; personally I do not think so.
The principal contributory causes are:
1.	The overdevelopment of railways beyond the immediate needs of the country.
Is the appointment of seven directors to the Canadian National railway system going to eliminate that fault?
2.	Aggressive and uncontrolled competition between two nation-wide railway enterprises, and competition the more disastrous in that one of the competitors was publicly-owned and supported by the full resources of the dominion.
Is the minister's measure going to overcome in any degree that unfortunate condition?
3.	The reactions of the world trade repression which began in 1929 and has progressively increased in its severity with each succeeding year.
The seven members of the board of directors will not improve that condition
4.	Competition from other forms of transport, notably road transport.
In- order to bring the report down to date we might also include air transport.
5.	Inelasticity of freight rates and railway practice generally which prevents prompt action in the meeting of falling revenues and dealing effectively with competition from other forms of transport.
6.	Contractual arrangements with labour organizations which set up a rigid wage scale and inflexible labour practices generally.
7.	The special disabilities of the Canadian National railways due to: -
(a)	assumption, through government action, of liabilities of insolvent railway systems for reasons of national credit.
(b)	large capital expenditures for improvement of the physical condition of the absorbed systems.
(c)	political and community pressure on the management arising out of direct government control.

C.N.R.-Board oj Directors
None of those seven contributory causes is going to be satisfactorily handled by the measure which has 'been introduced; in fact I fear that at least one of the causes suggested here is going to be severely aggravated by appointments such as these. I fear that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Howe) has erred. He is bringing the Canadian National system back to the realm of political control. I know he has not that in mind; I think possibly that is the thought furthest from his mind.
I am sure it is his hope and desire to administer the railways as he would administer a business of his own. Because of his lack of political experience, with which lack I can associate myself, no doubt that is his outlook, as it would be mine under similar conditions. But I want to assure the minister of this fact, that he is surrounded by a large number of men who are looking to the Canadian National Railways as a source of political influence. Through the Minister of Railways, who is to become the minister of transportation, and these seven directors who are to be appointed, these men hope to gain that political ascendancy that will help re-elect them from election to election and maintain the present government in power. I know the minister has not that in mind; I know he feels that I am exaggerating a possible condition, but I want to assure him that after having studied the measure he has introduced I can see on the horizon no other possibility than political control of our national railways, and the result is going to be worse chaos than we have at the present time. If the minister hopes and expects that the injection of a bit of business experience into the management of the Canadian National system will carry him through to a successful administration of these lines, I am afraid that he is labouring under a misapprehension; that within a reasonable length of time he will find that the criticism from this side of the house was well justified, and that he should have acted more in conformity with the recommendations contained in the Duff report than is the case with this bill.
This report urges cooperation.	That
cooperation has not so far been forthcoming. It also urges the elimination of competition, but competition has not been eliminated. It is a disgrace to this country to have two railway systems piling up deficits, unable to meet their current expenses and at the same time carrying on competition to the death, at the ultimate expense of the Canadian people. Many solutions have been suggested for our railway problem, but there is one point I want to make absolutely clear; other hon. members have emphasized this feeling and I want to stress it on my own behalf as
well as on behalf of hon. members on this side of the house. There is absolutely no thought in my mind of the amalgamation of our two great national systems. Of course I feel, as many other hon. members do, that we have in this dominion many, many miles of railway that we actually do not need. We are overdeveloped in that respect. The twentieth century was to be Canada's, and we built for Canada's century. But Canada's century, through no fault of our own, was stunted in its growth, and as a result we find ourselves with railway facilities adequate to meet the requirements of forty to fifty million people while we have a population of only eleven million to meet the cost. It is no wonder that we are piling up deficits, and I want to say to the minister that I do not think this bill is going to help in any way to solve this great problem now on our hands.
The government have suggested increased export and import trade as one means of overcoming this problem. That will help to a certain extent, but there is not enough import and export trade carried on by eleven million people to support the mileage that we have built and are operating at the present time. The only solution is to break down this competition by means of which the railways are gradually exterminating each other. Some of the great railway men of Canada have suggested solutions. I have emphasized the fact that I am unalterably opposed to amalgamation, and I think I speak for every member of the official opposition. I do not think there is anything on record to suggest that the Conservative party at any time stood for the amalgamation of these two great systems.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that knowing the Minister of Railways as I do, knowing his past experience in the business world and his immense capabilities as an executive, I expected that he would introduce into this assembly not a measure such as we have before us but a measure that would give leadership in the solution of this railway problem. I expected him to introduce a measure that would be commented upon for its boldness, but instead we have merely a return to the situation as it existed previously, a situation that was condemned not only by the Duff commission but by others interested in the solution of this great problem. I think what I hoped for was expected also by the people of this country, knowing the railway problem as they do. It has been suggested by some that the people of this country do not understand the railway problem, but that is not so; they do understand it. They are beginning to realize the seriousness of
C.N.R.-Board oj Directors

that problem, and I believe the Canadian people are ready for bold leadership looking to its solution. We are not going to return to prosperity unless we find a solution to this problem. We cannot continue to pile up debts at this rate, $85,000,000 in a single year. We cannot continue to have these millions of debt mounting up and survive. The government should give the leadership. The people of Canada did not expect such a measure to be introduced by this government. The Liberal party got the confidence of the people at the election last October; they were given the powers of government, the power to regulate and to legislate, but they have not used those powers to advantage. The Canadian people are disappointed; they were looking for courageous leadership and instead they are handed a dry bone, one sucked dry many years ago.
I expected the Minister of Railways to suggest to the house and to the country some great measure that would lead to the amelioration of the distress which we suffer in connection with our railways. I expected him to analyze carefully the recommendations made by our great railway men. I expected him to make some reference at least to the solution suggested by one of his colleagues, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), but I heard no reference to that solution. To my mind the Minister of Trade and Commerce offered a reasonable solution, one that would at least lead somewhere, not back to where we were in 1930. I think it was the Minister of Trade and Commerce who suggested the possibility of unification of these two great railways. Do not confuse unification with amalgamation; no one in his proper senses is suggesting amalgamation, but unification has its merits, and I expected that the Minister of Railways would at least discuss that phase of the subject so that the country at large and this house in particular would understand the government's position in regard to that possible solution. The people of this country are disappointed; they wanted to know what the government proposed to do and how they were going to solve this railway problem. If unification would solve it, why do the government not take the lead in that respect, particularly when they have at least one member in the cabinet who is definitely committed to such a solution?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Would the hon, member be good enough to explain the difference between unification and amalgamation?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Yes, it is very simple. The hon. member could have asked that question

of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) who was professor of economics at Queens; he could have given a more satisfactory answer than I. Amalgamation means the disappearance of both into a new unit; unification means the continuance of both units under one management until such time as this country grows and develops so that it can support the two separate railways. No great reasoning power is required to see through a plan of that kind. Of course there are difficulties in the way; I grant that. Any solution of any great problem has difficulties. I could name scores of difficulties in the way of unification of these railway systems, but I emphasize the seriousness of this railway problem; this country cannot continue to pile up deficits of $85,000,000 a year and survive. We have to find a solution, and that solution has to be found by the members of this government. They cannot allow this country to drift and drift into despair. Some people will suggest that unification of these railways would mean the possible elimination of a large number of men from their positions. If I thought for one moment that one man would lose his job on either railway through a process of unification I would be absolutely opposed to it. But I believe that a scheme can be worked out whereby under unification not one man would lose his job, whereby every man now employed with the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific would be retained in his position. It is on that account that I advocate a careful and close study on the part of the government of that suggested solution.
I could advance many statements in support of that idea, but as I do not want to take up the time of the house in doing so, I shall resist that temptation. I think I have made my position quite clear. The Minister of Railways has introduced a measure which is a reactionary and retrograde step. He would reestablish the board of directors in place of the board of trustees; that is running contrary to the recommendations of the Duff report. He is introducing again into the administration of the national railways the possibility, yes, the probability, of political patronage, and if there is anything that will continue to make our railway deficits higher and higher it is the meddling of politicians in appointments and in the way in which the railway is run.
Before this measure finally goes through I ask the minister to see if he cannot develop something that will give this house and this country more courageous leadership than we find in the measure at present before us. I know exactly his criticism of the present

C.N.R.-Board of Directors
personnel of the trustee boards; I know he has objections to certain individuals on it. But this is no solution for the trouble; he is only preparing for himself two and one-third times the trouble that he is probably experiencing at the present time. This is not a solution that the people of Canada expected from this government or from the present minister; it is a proposal1 that is most unacceptable to anyone who has made a careful and minute study of our railway problem. It is	a	stupendous	problem.	We shoulddivorce politics from railways entirely, look at it	as	a national	problem,	get togetherand find a solution. I do not see any reason why the government cannot invite the assistance of people on this side of the house to assist	in	solving the	problem.	The more Istudy	it	the more I	realize its	gigantic importance. Unless we can find a solution it is going to carry us down, so I hope the minister will realize the possibility that is before him at tihe present time to be hailed as a great liberator, not as the man who merely introduced a slight change in the management of our national railways in order to get rid of certain persons on the board of trustees. The people of Canada will be grateful to the minister if he can at least blaze a new trail that will lead us out of our present chaotic condition in connection with our railway and transportation system.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION BY BOARD OF DIRECTORS APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank hon. members in all parts of the house for the very fair discussion which this measure has received. I think everyone here is. impressed by the gravity of the situation with which we are dealing. I can assure hon. members that there is nothing with which I have ever had to do that has impressed me as being a more difficult and more serious problem than the one now before us. If anyone has the thought that the measure we have now before the house is the first step towards a program of extravagance, I ask him to dismiss it from his mind because that surely is not going to be the outcome.
Hon. members have expressed surprise that in bringing down this bill I have not offered a solution of the Canadian National Railway problem. Surely that is a little too much to expect from any man who is a layman, and in addition facing this problem at first hand and for the first time. There is no royal road, as I see it, to the solution of the Canadian National Railway problem. The trustee act was founded upon confidence in cooperation. Cooperation has been tested now for over two years, and it has not produced the results
which were expected from it. I am sure that everyone in this house regrets very much that more progress has not been made. But let us face the situation fairly. We have had the trustee system for the years 1934, 1935 and a small portion of 1936. In 1934 the cash requirements from the dominion government to keep the railway in operation, that is for deficits and capital expenditures- I make very little distinction between the two-was 856,000,000. In 1935, in spite of an increase of 88,000,000 of gross revenue, the requirements were $55,000,000. The budget first submitted for 1936 called for a further appropriation of $55,000,000 for this purpose. I am told that I set a precedent when I called the trustees to Ottawa and told them that as Minister of Railwaj's I must ask them to take a more optimistic view of the year 1936. We discussed the matter at some length, and as a result the requirements were cut down slightly below $50,000,000. Viewing the situation, it seems to me that 1935 was surely a good deal better than 1934 from every aspect, traffic as well as others, and surely 1936 will be a better year than 1935. Are we prepared to accept the view that the Canadian National Railway must draw in cash from the government of Canada some $50,000,000 or $55,000,000 every year? I think not. I think we must at least attack the problem in a different way.
The trusteeship, as hon. gentlemen know, was described as a bankruptcy situation. Well, the bankruptcy situation does not seem to be a solution, and in that respee' it is not much different from most bankruptcy situations. What happens in a bankruptcy situation is that a concern demonstrates that it cannot pay its way and is dissolved, or it demonstrates that it can pay its way and it is reorganized and is allowed to go back into normal business procedure. What we are doing by this bill-* and I believe it is a very important step- is bringing the road back out of bankruptcy and into business vitality. In doing so we are going to establish the ordinary business set-up of successful concerns in this country and elsewhere. We are going to restore management by experts in the railway business, with experience and qualifications that, we believe, will give the road expert technical direction. We are going to surround that expert direction with a board of directors which in business experience and in national respect, we believe will be the equal of the board of any other corporation in this country. In other words we are going to give the Canadian National Railways a chance as a business to go out and build. I say that we are going to give it a chance. We are going to give it the same chance that any business firm in Canada has.

Yes, pardon me. I was
speaking merely for the purpose of reference. But if that is the solution, it must involve tearing up not only the track but also the mortgage that built the track. I think the saving is lacking if only the rails come up without the mortgage that built them. I agree fully that if there are any further savings to be made in the way of economies that are practical-and after all tearing up four or five thousand miles of track is not practical-these savings should be made. I believe that the direction in which to look for the solution of the Canadian National Railway problem is on the constructive side, the building up of traffic and the pumping of vitality into the railway. That is the purpose of this legislation.
It has been said that the purpose of this legislation is to dismiss the present personnel of the board. That is not true. It is true that I do not think the personnel directing the road to-day has the proper business experience which was intended by the Duff report. However I may say that I tried to avoid the very thing I am facing to-day, this discussion of personnel. I saw each of the trustees soon after I came into office and explained to them the position as I see it to-day. I suggested that this unpleasantness could be avoided if they cared to resign. I have great respect for Judge Eullerton, who is a westerner like myself; at least we have often worked together in the same field. Mr. Morrow is a former client of mine, and in justice to him I .must say that when I put the situation to him he was quite willing to resign. However I saw no purpose in accepting one resignation unless all were prepared to do the same thing. The change in set-up would have gone on just the same, but this personal reference I have had to make would have been avoided.
